`@gentleduck/auth/oidc/op` lets other apps sign in through your engine. It mounts no routes: each method takes the parsed request and answers what to send.

It supports the authorization code flow with S256 PKCE, refresh tokens, ID tokens, userinfo, introspection (RFC 7662), revocation (RFC 7009) and dynamic client registration (RFC 7591). The code flow is the only one.

```ts
import { createOidcOP } from '@gentleduck/auth/oidc/op'

const op = createOidcOP({
  auth,
  config: { issuer: 'https://auth.example.com', supportedScopes: ['openid', 'profile', 'email', 'offline_access'] },
  signIdToken: (claims) => signJwt(claims),
})

const { client_secret } = await op.registerClient({
  client_id: 'web-app',
  redirect_uris: ['https://app.example.com/callback'],
  token_endpoint_auth_method: 'client_secret_basic',
})
```

`client_secret` is generated when you pass none, and returned only here; it is stored hashed. A client registered without a secret or an auth method is public, and must use PKCE.

## Routes

| Route | Call | Answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /authorize` | `op.authorize(query, { headers })` | `redirect`, `login_required`, `consent_required` or `error`, by `kind` |
| Your consent form | `op.completeConsent({ client_id, identity, redirect_uri, scope, sid, tenant_id, ... })` | The same, usually `redirect` with the code |
| `POST /token` | `op.token(body, headers)` | The tokens, or `{ error }` |
| `GET /userinfo` | `op.userinfo(headers)` | The claims, or `{ error }` |
| `POST /introspect` | `op.introspect(body, headers)` | `{ active, ... }` |
| `POST /revoke` | `op.revoke(body, headers)` | Nothing |
| `POST /register` | `op.register(body, headers)` | `{ status, body }` |

`headers` is a Fetch `Headers`. `authorize` finds the signed-in person through the engine's transport, so `login_required` means sending them to your sign-in page and back.

A code lives 10 minutes and works once. Access and ID tokens live an hour and refresh tokens 30 days; `config` changes each. A refresh token rotates on every use, and presenting a spent one revokes its whole family. Tokens are stored as SHA-256 hashes.

## Stores

The defaults are in memory. For production, pass the Drizzle stores for your dialect, from `oidc/op/drizzle/pg`, `mysql` or `sqlite`:

```ts
import { authCreateDrizzlePgOidcOpStores, authGcDrizzlePgOidcOp } from '@gentleduck/auth/oidc/op/drizzle/pg'

const op = createOidcOP({ auth, config, signIdToken, stores: authCreateDrizzlePgOidcOpStores(db) })

await authGcDrizzlePgOidcOp(db) // on a schedule; removes expired codes and tokens
```

## Dynamic registration

Off by default. Turn it on with a token that `POST /register` must carry as `Authorization: Bearer`:

```ts
const op = createOidcOP({
  auth,
  config,
  signIdToken,
  dcr: { enabled: true, initialAccessToken: process.env.OIDC_DCR_TOKEN, maxRedirectUris: 20 },
})
```

Without `initialAccessToken` anyone can register a client, so keep that behind a private network. Advertise the endpoint with `registrationEndpoint` in the [discovery document](/duck-auth/advanced/oidc).

A working provider with a consent page is in [`examples/oidc-op`](https://github.com/gentleeduck/duck-iam/tree/main/examples/oidc-op).

```ts
import { AuthWebhookDeliverer } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'

const webhooks = new AuthWebhookDeliverer({
  endpoints: [
    {
      url: 'https://hooks.example.com/auth',
      secret: process.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET ?? '',
      events: ['signin.success', 'session.revoked', 'mfa.enrolled'],
    },
  ],
  deadLetter: { put: async (entry) => saveFailedDelivery(entry) },
})

const detach = webhooks.attach(auth.events)
```

`attach` subscribes the deliverer to the events its endpoints name, and returns the call that detaches it. An emit does not wait for the delivery, so a slow receiver never slows a sign-in. On shutdown, `await webhooks.drain()` settles what is still in flight.

## Endpoints

| Field | Default | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `url` | required | HTTPS. Loopback, private, link-local and cloud-metadata hosts are refused at construction, and `allowInsecure: true` on the deliverer permits `http` for development only. |
| `secret` | required | Signs each request. |
| `events` | `'*'` | The [event names](/duck-auth/core/events) this endpoint receives. A name the engine never emits is refused. |
| `signatureHeader` | `X-Duck-Signature` | Where the signature goes. |
| `id` | the URL without its query | Names the endpoint in results and dead letters. |

The guard reads the host as written. Pass `resolveHost` to also check the addresses a name resolves to before each attempt; in Node, `(await lookup(host, { all: true })).map((a) => a.address)` from `node:dns/promises`.

## What is sent

A `POST` with the JSON body `{ deliveryId, event, payload, timestamp }`, where `timestamp` is when the event happened. Keys that carry a secret are removed from `payload` at any depth before it is signed; `redact` replaces that function. A body over 1 MiB is not sent.

| Header | |
| --- | --- |
| `X-Duck-Signature` | `authSha256=` and the hex HMAC-SHA256 of `` `${X-Duck-Timestamp}.${body}` `` |
| `X-Duck-Timestamp` | When this attempt was sent, in milliseconds. |
| `X-Duck-Delivery-Id` | The same on every attempt of one delivery. |

## Retries

A 2xx is delivered. A 408, a 429, any 5xx, a timeout (`timeoutMs`, 5 seconds) or a network failure is retried, up to `maxAttempts` (5) with exponential backoff from `backoffMs` (500 ms), jittered. Any other 4xx is not retried. A delivery that runs out goes to `deadLetter.put` with the endpoint, event, redacted payload, attempts and last error.

`webhooks.deliverOne(event, payload)` delivers one event by hand, for a replay, and answers per endpoint whether it landed.

## Receiving

Verify against the raw body, before parsing it:

```ts
import { authVerifyWebhookSignature } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'

app.post('/hooks/auth', express.text({ type: 'application/json' }), (req, res) => {
  const valid = authVerifyWebhookSignature(process.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET ?? '', req.body, req.get('x-duck-signature') ?? '', {
    timestamp: Number(req.get('x-duck-timestamp')),
  })
  if (!valid) return res.status(401).end()
  handle(JSON.parse(req.body))
  res.status(204).end()
})
```

* The check is constant-time, and refuses a timestamp more than `toleranceMs` (5 minutes) from now.
* Without `timestamp` it checks a signature over the bare body, which these requests never carry.
* A retry arrives with the same `X-Duck-Delivery-Id`. Record it to act once per delivery; the tolerance only bounds how late a replay can come.
* `authSignWebhookBody(secret, body, timestamp)` produces the header value, for testing a receiver.

## An engine for tests

```ts
import { createTest } from '@gentleduck/auth/test'
import { expect, it } from 'vitest'

it('signs in with the right password', async () => {
  const auth = createTest()
  const ada = await auth.identities.create({ profile: { username: 'ada', email: 'ada@example.com' } })
  await auth.passwords.set(ada.id, 'correct horse battery staple', auth.cfg.stores.credentials)

  const { sid, session } = await auth.flows.signIn({
    providerId: 'password',
    input: { email: 'ada@example.com', password: 'correct horse battery staple' },
  })

  expect(session?.identityId).toBe(ada.id)
  const resolved = await auth.resolveSession({ headers: new Headers({ authorization: `Bearer ${sid}` }) }).orNull()
  expect(resolved?.identity?.profile.email).toBe('ada@example.com')
})
```

`createTest()` is an engine over a `MemoryAdapter`, the bearer transport, a memory limiter allowing 1000 attempts a minute, and the password, MFA and API key providers. Each piece can be replaced:

```ts
import { MemoryLimiter } from '@gentleduck/auth/limiters/memory'

const auth = createTest({ limiter: new MemoryLimiter({ max: 2, windowMs: 60_000 }) })
// The third wrong password in a minute throws AUTH_RATE_LIMITED.
```

| Override | Replaces |
| --- | --- |
| `adapter`, `stores` | The memory adapter, or the whole store bag. |
| `transport`, `limiter`, `events` | Those engine pieces. |
| `providers` | Added after the three built in. |
| `passwords`, `mfa`, `apiKeys` | Those providers' options. |

`noopLimiter()` from `@gentleduck/auth/limiters/mock` never refuses, for a test that runs the same flow many times.

## Capturing what would be sent

```ts
import { MemoryAdapter } from '@gentleduck/auth/adapters/memory'
import { createAuth } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'
import { authTestDeliver } from '@gentleduck/auth/test'

const { deliver, outbox } = authTestDeliver()
const auth = createAuth({ baseUrl: 'https://app.example.com', stores: new MemoryAdapter(), deliver, strict: false })

const ada = await auth.identities.create({ profile: { username: 'ada', email: 'ada@example.com' } })
await auth.flows.requestEmailVerification({ identityId: ada.id })

expect(outbox[0]).toMatchObject({ kind: 'email-verification', identityId: ada.id })
const token = new URL(String(outbox[0]?.vars.url)).searchParams.get('token')
```

`outbox` holds every [message](/duck-auth/core/delivery) as `deliver` would have received it, with `identityId` and `tenantId` added.

## Redis

`fakeRedis()` from `@gentleduck/auth/test` is an in-memory client for the [`adapters/redis`](/duck-auth/adapters/redis) stores:

```ts
import { session } from '@gentleduck/auth/adapters/redis'
import { fakeRedis } from '@gentleduck/auth/test'

const sessions = session({ redis: fakeRedis() })
```

## The client

The client calls the `fetch` it is given, so a test can answer it directly:

```ts
import { createAuthClient } from '@gentleduck/auth/client/vanilla'

const client = createAuthClient({
  baseUrl: '/auth',
  fetch: async (url) =>
    String(url) === '/auth/session'
      ? Response.json({ session: null, identity: null })
      : Response.json({ ok: false, error: { code: 'AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS', status: 401 } }, { status: 401 }),
})
```

For component stories, the [Storybook decorator](/duck-auth/client/react#storybook) renders against a mock client.

A discovery document and a JWKS let another service verify the tokens your [JWT transport](/duck-auth/core/transports/jwt) signs without calling you. For a full OpenID provider, with `/authorize` and `/token`, see [OIDC provider](/duck-auth/advanced/oidc-op).

```ts
import { authBuildOidcDiscovery } from '@gentleduck/auth/oidc'

const discovery = authBuildOidcDiscovery({ issuer: 'https://auth.example.com', signingAlgs: ['ES256'] })

app.get('/.well-known/openid-configuration', (_req, res) => res.json(discovery))
app.get('/.well-known/jwks.json', (_req, res) => res.json(jwt.jwks()))
```

* `issuer` must be `https` unless `allowHttp: true`; a trailing slash is dropped.
* `signingAlgs` defaults to `['HS256']`; set it to your transport's algorithm. HS256 secrets never appear in the JWKS, so only an asymmetric key can be verified elsewhere.
* The OAuth endpoints it advertises sit under `prefix` (default `/auth`), and `jwks_uri` under `jwksPath` (default `/.well-known/jwks.json`). `extraClaims` adds fields but cannot replace these.
* Build the JWKS per request, so a key added by `rotateSignKey` appears. `authBuildOidcRoutes({ config, transport })` answers both documents at once, with the JWKS as of that call.

## Reading another issuer

```ts
import { authFetchOidcDiscovery } from '@gentleduck/auth/oidc'

const doc = await authFetchOidcDiscovery('https://accounts.example.com')
```

It fetches `/.well-known/openid-configuration` under the issuer, refuses `http` unless `allowHttp: true`, and caches the answer for an hour. `bypassCache: true` refetches, and `authFlushOidcDiscoveryCache()` empties the cache.

```ts
app.get('/.well-known/openid-configuration', (_req, res) => res.json(discovery))
app.get('/.well-known/jwks.json', (_req, res) => res.json(jwt.jwks()))
```

```ts
import { drizzlePgAdapter } from '@gentleduck/auth/adapters/drizzle/pg'
import { valkeyEvents, valkeySessionImpl } from '@gentleduck/auth/adapters/valkey'
import { createAuth } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'
import { valkeyLimiter } from '@gentleduck/auth/limiters/valkey'
import { passwords } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/passwords'
import Redis from 'ioredis'

const redis = new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL ?? '')
const sql = drizzlePgAdapter(process.env.DATABASE_URL ?? '')

export const auth = createAuth({
  baseUrl: 'https://app.example.com',
  stores: { identities: sql.identities, credentials: sql.credentials, sessions: valkeySessionImpl({ redis }) },
  limiter: valkeyLimiter({ redis }),
  events: valkeyEvents({ cmd: redis, sub: new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL ?? '') }),
  providers: [passwords()],
  strict: false,
})

auth.events.on('lockout', (event) => alertOps(event))
auth.strict({ env: 'production' })
```

`createAuth` runs `strict()` as it returns, for the env named by `strict` or else `NODE_ENV`, falling back to `development`. Production requires a `lockout` listener, which cannot exist before `createAuth` returns, so a production engine opts out there and calls `strict()` once it is subscribed.

Outside production, `strict()` checks only the [compliance preset](/duck-auth/core/compliance), if one is set. A failure throws one `AUTH_MISCONFIGURED` whose `meta.detail` lists every problem.

## What production refuses

| Area | Refused |
| --- | --- |
| Limiter | None, `NoopLimiter`, or the in-process `MemoryLimiter`. |
| Stores | A memory store in any `stores` slot. |
| Events | No bus, or the in-process one. |
| Captcha | The null verifier, which passes everything, or a siteverify endpoint over `http`. |
| Transport | A cookie transport with `secure: false`, or a JWT transport signing HS256 with a key under 32 bytes. A composite's parts are checked one by one. |
| OAuth | A `stateSigningSecret` under 32 bytes, or `allowStateReplay: true`. |
| Passkey | The in-process challenge store. |
| Magic link | No `deliver`, so no link could be sent. |
| Passwords | A hasher below its own defaults: scrypt `N` under 2^14, `r` under 8 or `keylen` under 32; Argon2id `memoryCost` under 19456, `timeCost` under 2 or `hashLength` under 32. |
| Engine | A `baseUrl` that is not `https`, no provider, or no `lockout` listener. |

A store, transport, provider or hasher of your own publishes none of the markers these checks read, so it is not judged.

The in-process pieces are refused because a second instance cannot see them: a limiter budget is granted once per instance, and a revocation, OAuth `state` or passkey challenge used on one instance stays live on the others. [Redis and Valkey](/duck-auth/adapters/redis) has the shared versions.

Reporting, scope and a deployment checklist are in [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/gentleeduck/duck-iam/blob/main/packages/duck-auth/SECURITY.md).

content:
One engine serves every tenant. Identities are global: one person, one row, one email across all of them. What carries a tenant is what they hold in it:

* **Credentials.** A password, TOTP secret, passkey or API key belongs to the tenant it was created under.
* **Sessions.** A session records the tenant it was signed in to.

## Signing in to a tenant

```ts
await auth.passwords.set(ada.id, password, auth.cfg.stores.credentials, { tenantId: 'acme' })

const { sid, session } = await auth.flows.signIn({ providerId: 'password', input: { email, password }, tenantId: 'acme' })
// session.tenantId === 'acme'
```

A sign-in under `globex` does not find acme's password and answers `AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS`.

## Resolving under a tenant

```ts
const resolved = await auth.resolveSession(req, { expectedTenantId: 'acme' }).orNull()
```

A session from another tenant resolves as absent. The [CSRF guards](/duck-auth/server#your-own-routes) take the same option: `csrfGuard(auth, req, { expectedTenantId })`, `expressCsrf(auth, { expectedTenantId })`.

## Leaving the tenant out

A call without a tenant is unscoped, not scoped to "no tenant":

* A sign-in without `tenantId` finds a credential in any tenant, and its session records none.
* A resolve without `expectedTenantId` accepts a session from any tenant.
* `auth.sessions.listForIdentity(id)` lists the person's sessions in every tenant. Pass `{ tenantId }` to list one.

So the mounted [server routes](/duck-auth/server), which pass no tenant, serve a single-tenant app. A multi-tenant app writes its sign-in route and its guards itself, with the tenant from the host or path; [Fetch runtimes](/duck-auth/server/generic) has a sign-in route to start from.

## The ambient tenant

`withTenant(tenantId, fn)` binds a tenant for everything `fn` awaits, `currentTenant()` reads it, and `resolveTenant(explicit)` answers the explicit one when given and the bound one otherwise. They are for your own code. No engine call reads the bound tenant, so each still needs its `tenantId` passed.

```ts
import { resolveTenant, withTenant } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'

app.use((req, _res, next) => withTenant(req.hostname.split('.')[0], next))

// In a handler below it:
const { tenantId } = resolveTenant()
await auth.flows.signIn({ providerId: 'password', input, tenantId })
```

Organisations inside a tenant, with members and roles, are the [orgs facet](/duck-auth/core/orgs).

content:
Auth for a TypeScript backend comes three ways: a hosted service that runs it for you (Clerk, WorkOS, Stytch), a framework's own solution (Auth.js), or a library you run yourself. duck-auth is a library you run yourself, in your process and against your database, with the providers, transports and stores already written.

## What it ships

| Area | In the package |
| --- | --- |
| Sign-in | Passwords, magic links, OAuth (Apple, Discord, GitHub, Google, LinkedIn, Microsoft, or any other through `providers/oauth/core`), passkeys, API keys, SAML. |
| Second factors | TOTP, backup codes, WebAuthn; step-up to AAL 2 and remembered devices. |
| Sessions | Cookie, bearer and JWT transports (HS256, ES256, RS256, EdDSA, with key rotation and a JWKS), DPoP, hijack and anomaly detection, impersonation. |
| Storage | Drizzle on Postgres, MySQL and SQLite; Redis and Valkey for sessions, limits and events; an in-memory adapter for tests. |
| Servers | Express, Fastify, Hono, Koa, Elysia, Next.js, NestJS, gRPC, and any fetch runtime. |
| Clients | Vanilla, React, Vue, Svelte, Solid. |
| Operations | Multi-tenancy, organisations, signed webhooks, encryption at rest, GDPR, HIPAA, SOC 2 and FIPS presets, and a `strict()` gate that refuses a production engine built with development pieces. |

## What it leaves out

* **Hosting.** There is no service and no dashboard; you run it and own the data.
* **UI.** The clients hold session state and call the server. The forms are yours.
* **Authorization.** It says who the caller is, never what they may do. That is [duck-iam](/duck-iam/introduction); see [Bridging to duck-iam](/duck-auth/guides/iam-bridge).
* **SMS codes.** There is no SMS second factor; SIM swaps make it a weak one. Your [`deliver`](/duck-auth/core/delivery) function can still send links by SMS.

## Choosing

* Pick a hosted service to run nothing and to get prebuilt sign-in screens, at the price of per-user billing and your users living in someone else's database.
* Pick a smaller library to write the providers and flows yourself.
* Pick duck-auth to own the runtime and the data without writing the providers, flows and stores.

content:
A password is one way in. This chapter adds two more: a link mailed to the address, and GitHub. Both end in the same kind of session, so nothing downstream changes.

## Learning goals

* Register a provider that needs the engine's `deliver`.
* Redeem a magic link from a page the person clicks through.
* Configure GitHub and write the OAuth callback route.
* Know when an OAuth sign-in links to an existing account.

## The OAuth round trip

<MermaidDiagram
  chart={`sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant X as DuckNotes
  participant G as GitHub
  B->>X: POST /auth/providers/oauth:github/begin
  X-->>B: url to GitHub, pre-auth cookie duck-oauth
  B->>G: authorize
  G-->>B: redirect to the callback with code and state
  B->>X: GET /auth/providers/oauth:github/callback
  X->>G: exchange the code, read the profile
  X-->>B: session cookies, redirect to /`}
/>

## Step by step

<Steps>
<Step>Register both providers</Step>

```ts title="src/auth.ts"
import { MemoryAdapter } from '@gentleduck/auth/adapters/memory'
import { createAuth, orNull } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'
import { cookieTransport, memoryDPoPNonceStore } from '@gentleduck/auth/core/transport'
import { magicLink } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/magic-link'
import { github } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/oauth/github'
import { passwords } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/passwords'
import { deliver } from './mailer'

const stores = new MemoryAdapter()

export const auth = createAuth({
  baseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
  deliver,
  stores,
  transport: cookieTransport({ name: 'sid', secure: false }),
  providers: [
    passwords(),
    (_engine, send) =>
      magicLink({
        callbackPath: '/magic-link',
        deliver: send,
        findIdentityByEmail: (email) => orNull(stores.identities.find({ email })),
      }),
    github({
      clientId: process.env.GITHUB_CLIENT_ID ?? '',
      clientSecret: process.env.GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET ?? '',
      redirectUri: 'http://localhost:3000/auth/providers/oauth:github/callback',
      stateSigningSecret: process.env.OAUTH_STATE_SECRET ?? '',
      stateCookie: { name: 'duck-oauth', secure: false },
      nonceStore: memoryDPoPNonceStore(),
      profileToIdentityProfile: (p) => (p.email ? { email: p.email, username: `github:${p.sub}` } : null),
      onFederationConflict: 'link-if-verified',
    }),
  ],
})
```

* `stateCookie` gets a plain name and `secure: false` for http, as the session cookie did in chapter 1.
* `nonceStore` burns each `state` once, so a callback URL copied from history cannot sign in again. The memory store serves one process; chapter 8 moves it to Valkey.
* `profileToIdentityProfile` builds the profile for someone GitHub sends who has no account yet.

<Step>The callback route</Step>

In `src/server.ts`, import `AuthError` from `@gentleduck/auth/core`, `applyIntents` and `expressCaller` from `@gentleduck/auth/server/express`, and `oauthCallback` beside `errorToHttp`. Change the static line to serve `.html` pages without the extension, and add the callback next to the mounted routes:

```ts title="src/server.ts"
app.use(express.static('public', { extensions: ['html'] }))

app.get('/auth/providers/:id/callback', async (req, res) => {
  try {
    const request = { cookie: req.headers.cookie, method: req.method, url: req.url }

    applyIntents([...intents, { type: 'redirect', url: '/' }], res)
  } catch (err) {
    res.redirect(`/?error=${err instanceof AuthError ? err.code : 'AUTH_PROVIDER_FAILED'}`)
  }
})
```

<Step>The page</Step>

```html title="public/index.html"

```


```ts title="src/page.ts"
  linkForm.hidden = Boolean(identity)
```

and wire them at the end:

```ts title="src/page.ts"

```

```html title="public/magic-link.html"

<meta charset="utf-8" />
<title>DuckNotes</title>
<button>Finish signing in</button>
<script type="module" src="/magic-link.js"></script>
```

## What just happened

1. **Sending a link answered the same for anyone.** `beginProvider('magic-link')` answers `{ ok: true }` whether or not the address has an account, and the server printed a link to `/magic-link?token=...` only for Ada.
2. **The link signs in on a click, not on load.** Mail scanners open links to check them; a page that signed in on load would spend the token before the person got there.
3. **Redeeming the link proved the address.** Ada's identity is now `emailVerified`. If it was not before, the link also removed everything else on the account, her password included: until that moment, anyone could have signed up with her address and set it.
4. **GitHub's begin answered a URL, not a redirect.** The client asks for JSON, so the begin route answers `{ url }` and the client sends the page there, carrying the `duck-oauth` cookie that binds the flow to this browser.
5. **The callback found Ada's account.** GitHub said her primary address is verified, and so had duck-auth, so `'link-if-verified'` linked GitHub to the existing identity. The session's factor is `oauth`.

## Who an OAuth sign-in becomes

| Situation | Result |
| --- | --- |
| This GitHub account is already linked | That identity signs in. |
| An account owns the email, and both sides verified it | Linked, with `'link-if-verified'`. |
| An account owns the email, and either side did not verify it | Refused with `AUTH_PROVIDER_FAILED`. The default `'reject'` refuses every such case. |
| No account owns the email | `profileToIdentityProfile` creates one, with `emailVerified: false`. |

## Try it

1. Sign up a new account with a password and, without verifying it, sign in with GitHub under the same address. The callback redirects to `/?error=AUTH_PROVIDER_FAILED`.
2. Click the same magic link twice. The second click shows `AUTH_RECOVERY_TOKEN_INVALID`.
3. Request two links in a row and use the first. A newer link replaces the older one.

```

    magic-link.html - where the link lands
  src/
    auth.ts         - password, magic link, GitHub
    server.ts       - plus the OAuth callback
    page.ts
    magic-link.ts
```

* [GitHub](/duck-auth/providers/oauth/github): what the preset reads.

This chapter adds a code from an authenticator app, required where losing the account would hurt: deleting her notes. ## Learning goals * Enroll TOTP and show the backup codes once. * Refuse a route until the session is at AAL 2, and was proven recently. * Step a session up with a code or a backup code. ## Stepping up >X: DELETE /api/notes, session at AAL 1 X-->>B: 403 AUTH_STEP_UP_REQUIRED B->>X: POST /api/step-up with a code X-->>B: new sid at AAL 2 B->>X: DELETE /api/notes X-->>B: 204`} /> ## Step by step Register the MFA provider ```ts title="src/auth.ts" import { mfaProvider } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/mfa' export const auth = createAuth({ // ... providers: [ passwords(), mfaProvider({ issuer: 'DuckNotes' }), // the magic link and GitHub, as in chapter 6 ], }) ``` `issuer` is the name the authenticator app lists the account under. Enrollment, step-up, and a guarded route Add to `src/server.ts`, after the notes routes: ```ts title="src/server.ts" app.post('/api/mfa/totp', async (_req, res) => { const { uri } = await auth.mfa.beginTotpEnrollment(res.locals.identity.id, res.locals.identity.profile.email) res.json({ uri }) }) app.post('/api/mfa/totp/confirm', async (req, res) => { const confirmed = await auth.mfa.confirmTotpEnrollment(res.locals.identity.id, String(req.body.code)) if (!confirmed.ok) return res.status(400).json({ code: 'AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS' }) res.json({ backupCodes: confirmed.backupCodes }) }) app.post('/api/step-up', async (req, res) => { const { intents } = await auth.flows.completeStepUp({ currentSid: auth.transport.extract({ headers: toHeaders(req.headers) }) ?? '', method: req.body.method === 'backup-code' ? 'backup-code' : 'totp', code: String(req.body.code), ...expressCaller(req), }) applyIntents(intents, res) }) app.delete('/api/notes', async (_req, res) => { const need = await auth.flows.checkStepUp(res.locals.session, { methods: ['totp', 'backup-code'], freshness: 5 * 60_000 }) if (!need.satisfied) return res.status(403).json({ code: 'AUTH_STEP_UP_REQUIRED', methods: need.methods }) notes.delete(res.locals.identity.id) res.status(204).end() }) ``` A stand-in for the authenticator app ```ts title="src/code.ts" import { totpAt } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/mfa' console.log(totpAt(process.argv[2] ?? '', Math.floor(Date.now() / 30_000))) ``` It prints the current code for a secret, as the app would. A real page renders the enrollment `uri` as a QR code for the app to scan. Drive it with curl Restart the server, sign up and sign in as in chapter 4, then start enrolling: ```bash csrf() { awk '7 }' jar; } curl -s -b jar localhost:3000/api/mfa/totp -X POST -H "x-csrf-token: $(csrf)" # {"uri":"otpauth://totp/DuckNotes%3Aada%40example.com?secret=YE2AT4YF...&issuer=DuckNotes&..."} ``` Confirm with the current code for that secret. The answer holds the backup codes: ```bash curl -s -b jar localhost:3000/api/mfa/totp/confirm -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -H "x-csrf-token: (npx tsx src/code.ts )\"}" # {"backupCodes":["33zh6-627z6","u7hpa-e8tnj",...]} ``` Deleting the notes is refused, because the session is still the password's: ```bash curl -s -b jar localhost:3000/api/notes -X DELETE -H "x-csrf-token: $(csrf)" # {"code":"AUTH_STEP_UP_REQUIRED","methods":["totp","backup-code"]} ``` Wait for the code to change, step up with the new one, and delete again: ```bash curl -s -b jar -c jar localhost:3000/api/step-up -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -H "x-csrf-token: (npx tsx src/code.ts )\"}" curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -b jar localhost:3000/api/notes -X DELETE -H "x-csrf-token: $(csrf)" # 204 ``` ## What just happened 1. **Enrolling stored the secret unconfirmed.** `beginTotpEnrollment` answered the `otpauth://` URI, but the secret is not a factor until a code proves the app holds it. 2. **Confirming minted ten backup codes.** They are stored hashed, so that answer is the only time they can be shown. Each stands in for a code once, for someone who lost the phone. 3. **Sign-in did not change.** The password still answers a session at AAL 1. `checkStepUp` is where the second factor is required: AAL 2 by default, and with `freshness`, a factor presented in the last five minutes. 4. **The confirming code could not step up.** Every code works once, so the step-up waited for the next. 5. **Stepping up rotated the session.** `completeStepUp` checked the code and minted a new sid at AAL 2, which `applyIntents` set along with a new `duck-csrf`. The old sid still works at AAL 1, so another tab is not signed out. ## Try it 1. Step up with the code `000000`. The answer is 401 `AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS`, and the session stays at AAL 1. 2. Step up with a backup code (`"method":"backup-code"`), then with the same one again. The second is refused. 3. Start enrolling again. It is refused with `AUTH_MFA_REQUIRED`: replacing a factor means removing it first with `auth.mfa.removeTotp`, behind the same `checkStepUp`. 4. Set `freshness` to `10_000`, step up, and wait ten seconds before deleting. The answer is 403 again, because the factor is no longer fresh. ## Where we are ``` ducknotes/ public/ index.html magic-link.html src/ mailer.ts auth.ts - now with the MFA provider server.ts - plus enrollment, step-up and a guarded delete code.ts - the authenticator app's stand-in page.ts magic-link.ts ``` ## See also * [Adding MFA](/duck-auth/guides/mfa): removing a factor, WebAuthn as a factor, remembered devices. * [Sessions](/duck-auth/core/sessions#rotation): what a step-up keeps of the old session. * [Flows](/duck-auth/core/flows): `checkStepUp` and `completeStepUp` in full. * [Chapter 8: production](/duck-auth/course/chapter-8)

The answer holds the backup codes: ```bash curl -s -b jar localhost:3000/api/mfa/totp/confirm -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -H "x-csrf-token: (npx tsx src/code.ts )\"}" # {"backupCodes":["33zh6-627z6","u7hpa-e8tnj",...]} ``` Deleting the notes is refused, because the session is still the password's: ```bash curl -s -b jar localhost:3000/api/notes -X DELETE -H "x-csrf-token: $(csrf)" # {"code":"AUTH_STEP_UP_REQUIRED","methods":["totp","backup-code"]} ``` Wait for the code to change, step up with the new one, and delete again: ```bash curl -s -b jar -c jar localhost:3000/api/step-up -H 'content-type: application/json' \ -H "x-csrf-token: (npx tsx src/code.ts )\"}" curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -b jar localhost:3000/api/notes -X DELETE -H "x-csrf-token: $(csrf)" # 204 ``` ## What just happened 1. **Enrolling stored the secret unconfirmed.** `beginTotpEnrollment` answered the `otpauth://` URI, but the secret is not a factor until a code proves the app holds it. 2. **Confirming minted ten backup codes.** They are stored hashed, so that answer is the only time they can be shown. Each stands in for a code once, for someone who lost the phone. 3. **Sign-in did not change.** The password still answers a session at AAL 1. `checkStepUp` is where the second factor is required: AAL 2 by default, and with `freshness`, a factor presented in the last five minutes. 4. **The confirming code could not step up.** Every code works once, so the step-up waited for the next. 5. **Stepping up rotated the session.** `completeStepUp` checked the code and minted a new sid at AAL 2, which `applyIntents` set along with a new `duck-csrf`. The old sid still works at AAL 1, so another tab is not signed out. ## Try it 1. Step up with the code `000000`. The answer is 401 `AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS`, and the session stays at AAL 1. 2. Step up with a backup code (`"method":"backup-code"`), then with the same one again. The second is refused. 3. Start enrolling again. It is refused with `AUTH_MFA_REQUIRED`: replacing a factor means removing it first with `auth.mfa.removeTotp`, behind the same `checkStepUp`. 4. Set `freshness` to `10_000`, step up, and wait ten seconds before deleting. The answer is 403 again, because the factor is no longer fresh. ## Where we are ``` ducknotes/ public/ index.html magic-link.html src/ mailer.ts auth.ts - now with the MFA provider server.ts - plus enrollment, step-up and a guarded delete code.ts - the authenticator app's stand-in page.ts magic-link.ts ``` ## See also * [Adding MFA](/duck-auth/guides/mfa): removing a factor, WebAuthn as a factor, remembered devices. * [Sessions](/duck-auth/core/sessions#rotation): what a step-up keeps of the old session. * [Flows](/duck-auth/core/flows): `checkStepUp` and `completeStepUp` in full. * [Chapter 8: production](/duck-auth/course/chapter-8)

content:
This course builds the authentication for **DuckNotes**, a small notes app, one chapter at a time. Every chapter adds to the same source tree, and every snippet runs as shown against `@gentleduck/auth`.

## What you build

<MermaidDiagram
  chart={`flowchart LR
  B["Browser: sign-in form, notes page"] --> X["Express server"]
  X --> E["AuthEngine"]
  E --> ST["Stores: identities, credentials, sessions"]
  E --> M["deliver: your mailer"]
  X --> N["Notes API"]`}
/>

By the end, people sign up, verify their address, sign in with a password, a mailed link or GitHub, add a TOTP second factor, and must step up before a destructive action. It all runs on Postgres and Valkey behind a `strict()` production check.

## The roadmap

<MermaidDiagram
  chart={`flowchart LR
  subgraph CORE["Part 1 - the engine"]
      direction LR
      C1["1. First sign-in"] --> C2["2. Accounts"]
      C2 --> C3["3. Sessions"]
  end
  subgraph SHIP["Part 2 - the app"]
      direction LR
      C4["4. HTTP"] --> C5["5. The browser"]
      C5 --> C6["6. More ways in"]
      C6 --> C7["7. A second factor"]
      C7 --> C8["8. Production"]
  end
  CORE --> SHIP`}
/>

Part 1 drives the engine from a script, so every answer is printed. Part 2 puts it behind HTTP and a browser, then hardens it.

## Course map

| Chapter | Topic | What you learn |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [1](/duck-auth/course/chapter-1) | Your first sign-in | `createAuth`, identities, passwords, `signIn`, `resolveSession`, `AuthError` |
| [2](/duck-auth/course/chapter-2) | Accounts | `deliver`, email verification, password reset, events |
| [3](/duck-auth/course/chapter-3) | Sessions | The row, deadlines, rotation, devices, hijack detection |
| [4](/duck-auth/course/chapter-4) | Behind HTTP | The Express handlers, your own routes, CSRF, `errorToHttp` |
| [5](/duck-auth/course/chapter-5) | In the browser | The vanilla client, envelopes, the CSRF cookie, React |
| [6](/duck-auth/course/chapter-6) | More ways in | Magic links, GitHub OAuth, account linking |
| [7](/duck-auth/course/chapter-7) | A second factor | TOTP enrollment, backup codes, step-up to AAL 2 |
| [8](/duck-auth/course/chapter-8) | Production | Postgres, Valkey, `strict()`, tests |

## Prerequisites

* TypeScript and `async`/`await`.
* Node.js 22 or newer, or Bun.
* No database until chapter 8, which uses Postgres and Valkey.

## Setup

<Steps>
<Step>Create the project</Step>

```bash
mkdir ducknotes && cd ducknotes
npm init -y
npm pkg set type=module
mkdir src
```

<Step>Install duck-auth</Step>

<PackageManagerTabs bun="bun add @gentleduck/auth @node-rs/argon2" npm="npm i @gentleduck/auth @node-rs/argon2" pnpm="pnpm add @gentleduck/auth @node-rs/argon2" yarn="yarn add @gentleduck/auth @node-rs/argon2" />

`@node-rs/argon2` is the password hasher's peer. Everything else is installed by the chapter that needs it.

<Step>Add a runner</Step>

```bash
npm i -D tsx
npx tsx src/main.ts
```

<Step>Start</Step>

Go to [Chapter 1: your first sign-in](/duck-auth/course/chapter-1).
</Steps>

## How the chapters are written

Each chapter has **learning goals**, a **diagram** of what it introduces, the **code**, **what just happened** inside the engine, and a **try it** exercise. New concepts link to their reference page.

<Callout tone="info" title="Version">
The code is verified against `@gentleduck/auth` 5.13.0. Import paths come from the package `exports` map: `@gentleduck/auth/core`, `@gentleduck/auth/adapters/memory`, `@gentleduck/auth/server/express` and so on.
</Callout>

## See also

* [Introduction](/duck-auth/introduction): the same ground as reference.
* [Quick start](/duck-auth/guides): one Express file, without the tour.
* [Concepts](/duck-auth/concepts): the terms the course uses.

The server from chapter 4 is complete; now a page talks to it. The client wraps the routes you mounted, so the page never builds a sign-in request or parses a cookie by hand, except for the one request that is yours. ## Learning goals * Create a client with `createAuthClient` and match it to the server. * Read an envelope instead of catching an error. * Keep the page in step with the session through `onChange`. * Send the CSRF token on a request the client does not make. ## Where the client sits C["createAuthClient"] C --> |"POST /auth/signin, GET /auth/session"| X["Express"] P --> |"fetch /api/notes with x-csrf-token"| X C --> |"onChange"| P`} /> ## Step by step Serve a page Add one line to `src/server.ts`, under `express.json()`: ```ts title="src/server.ts" app.use(express.static('public')) ``` ```html title="public/index.html" DuckNotes

Loading

    ``` The page script ```ts title="src/page.ts" import { createAuthClient } from '@gentleduck/auth/client/vanilla' type Profile = { username: string; email: string } const client = createAuthClient({ baseUrl: '/auth', csrfCookieName: 'duck-csrf' }) const status = document.querySelector('#status') const list = document.querySelector('#notes') const signInForm = document.querySelector('#sign-in') const noteForm = document.querySelector('#note') const signOut = document.querySelector('#sign-out') if (!status || !list || !signInForm || !noteForm || !signOut) throw new Error('DuckNotes markup is missing') const showNotes = async () => { const res = await fetch('/api/notes') const notes: string[] = res.ok ? await res.json() : [] list.replaceChildren(...notes.map((text) => Object.assign(document.createElement('li'), { textContent: text }))) } client.onChange(({ identity }) => { status.textContent = identity ? `Signed in as ${identity.profile.email}` : 'Signed out' signInForm.hidden = Boolean(identity) noteForm.hidden = !identity void showNotes() }) signInForm.addEventListener('submit', async (event) => { event.preventDefault() const form = new FormData(signInForm) const res = await client.signIn({ providerId: 'password', input: { email: form.get('email'), password: form.get('password') }, }) if (!res.ok) status.textContent = res.error.code === 'AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS' ? 'Wrong email or password' : 'Try again' }) noteForm.addEventListener('submit', async (event) => { event.preventDefault() const csrfToken = document.cookie.match(/(?:^|; )duck-csrf=([^;]*)/)?.[1] ?? '' await fetch('/api/notes', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json', 'x-csrf-token': csrfToken }, body: JSON.stringify({ text: new FormData(noteForm).get('text') }), }) noteForm.reset() await showNotes() }) signOut.addEventListener('click', () => client.signOut()) await client.getSession() ``` Bundle it and open the page ```bash npm i -D esbuild npx esbuild src/page.ts --bundle --format=esm --outfile=public/page.js npx tsx src/server.ts ``` Open `http://localhost:3000`, sign up Ada with the curl call from chapter 4, then sign in from the page.     ## What just happened 1. **`getSession` read the session once on load,** and `onChange` drew the page from it. Every later sign-in and sign-out notifies the same listener, so there is one place that decides what is shown. 2. **A wrong password was an envelope, not a throw.** Every client call answers `{ ok: true, data }` or `{ ok: false, error }`, with `error.code` as the server wrote it. A request that never reached the server answers `AUTH_NETWORK_ERROR`. 3. **The client sent the CSRF token on sign-out by itself.** It reads the `duck-csrf` cookie and echoes it in `x-csrf-token` on every write it makes. The notes request is yours, so it does the same by hand. 4. **`csrfCookieName: 'duck-csrf'` matches the server.** Over https with the default cookie settings the cookie is `__Host-duck-csrf`, which is also the client's default. Chapter 8 drops the option. 5. **The session cookie stayed out of reach.** `sid` is HttpOnly, so no script on the page, yours or an injected one, can read it. `duck-csrf` is readable on purpose. ## The same in React `@gentleduck/auth/client/react` wraps the same client in a provider and hooks: ```tsx title="src/header.tsx" import { Provider, useSession, useSignOut } from '@gentleduck/auth/client/react' type Profile = { username: string; email: string } function Header() { const { data, status } = useSession() const signOut = useSignOut() if (status === 'loading') return null if (status === 'guest') return Sign in return } export function App() { return (
    ) } ``` Vue, Svelte and Solid have the same shape; see [Client libraries](/duck-auth/client). ## Try it 1. Sign in, then reload. The notes come back, because the page asks the server rather than remembering anything. 2. Delete the `duck-csrf` cookie in the dev tools and add a note. The server answers 403 `AUTH_CSRF`. 3. Stop the server and sign in. `res.error.code` is `AUTH_NETWORK_ERROR`, and the page says "Try again". ## Where we are ``` ducknotes/ public/ index.html page.js - built from src/page.ts src/ mailer.ts auth.ts server.ts - now serving public/ page.ts - the browser client ``` ## See also * [Client libraries](/duck-auth/client): envelopes and matching the server. * [Vanilla client](/duck-auth/client/vanilla): every option and method. * [React client](/duck-auth/client/react): the hooks and the Storybook decorator. * [Chapter 6: more ways in](/duck-auth/course/chapter-6)

content: Until now the engine answered a script. This chapter puts it behind Express, where the session travels as a cookie and every response is built from the engine's intents. ## Learning goals * Mount the sign-in, sign-out, session and provider routes. * Write the routes that are yours: sign-up, verification, reset. * Guard your own routes with the session and the CSRF check. * Turn any thrown `AuthError` into a response with `errorToHttp`. ## One request >X: POST /auth/signin with email and password X->>E: flows.signIn E-->>X: intents: set sid, set duck-csrf X-->>B: 200 with two Set-Cookie headers B->>X: POST /api/notes with cookies and x-csrf-token X->>E: CSRF check, resolveSession E-->>X: Ada's session X-->>B: 201`} /> The engine never touches Express's response. It answers **intents** (set this cookie, redirect there, send this JSON), and the Express adapter applies them. ## Step by step Install Express ```bash npm i express npm i -D @types/express ``` Print the links The server has no outbox to read, so the mailer prints each link where you can copy it: ```ts title="src/mailer.ts" import type { Deliver } from '@gentleduck/auth/core' export const deliver: Deliver = async ({ kind, identity, vars }) => { console.log(`[${kind}] ${identity.profile.email}: ${vars.url}`) } ``` `src/auth.ts` stays as it was at the end of chapter 2, without the listeners. The server ```ts title="src/server.ts" import { orNull } from '@gentleduck/auth/core' import { expressCsrf, mountProviderBegin, mountSession, mountSignIn, mountSignOut, toHeaders, } from '@gentleduck/auth/server/express' import { errorToHttp } from '@gentleduck/auth/server/generic' import express, { type ErrorRequestHandler } from 'express' import { auth } from './auth' const notes = new Map() const app = express() app.use(express.json()) app.post('/auth/signin', mountSignIn(auth)) app.post('/auth/signout', mountSignOut(auth)) app.get('/auth/session', mountSession(auth)) app.post('/auth/providers/:id/begin', mountProviderBegin(auth)) app.use(expressCsrf(auth)) app.post('/auth/signup', async (req, res) => { const { email, password } = req.body auth.passwords.assertStrength(password) const identity = await auth.identities.create({ profile: { email, username: email } }) await auth.passwords.set(identity.id, password, auth.cfg.stores.credentials) await auth.flows.requestEmailVerification({ identityId: identity.id }) res.status(201).json({ identityId: identity.id }) }) app.post('/auth/verify-email', async (req, res) => { await auth.flows.completeEmailVerification({ token: String(req.body.token) }) res.status(204).end() }) app.post('/auth/forgot-password', async (req, res) => { await auth.flows.requestPasswordReset({ input: { email: String(req.body.email) }, findIdentityByEmail: (email) => orNull(auth.identities.getByEmail(email)), }) res.status(202).end() }) app.post('/auth/reset-password', async (req, res) => { await auth.flows.completePasswordReset({ token: String(req.body.token), newPassword: String(req.body.password) }) res.status(204).end() }) app.use('/api', async (req, res, next) => { const resolved = await auth.resolveSession({ headers: toHeaders(req.headers) }).orNull() if (!resolved?.identity) return res.status(401).end() res.locals.session = resolved.session res.locals.identity = resolved.identity next() }) app.get('/api/notes', (_req, res) => { res.json(notes.get(res.locals.identity.id) ?? []) }) app.post('/api/notes', (req, res) => { const mine = notes.get(res.locals.identity.id) ?? content:
DuckNotes starts with one question: who is making this request? This chapter builds the smallest engine that can answer it, signs Ada in, and takes the answer apart.

## Learning goals

* Build an `AuthEngine` with `createAuth` from a store, a transport and a provider.
* Create an identity and give it a password.
* Sign in with `auth.flows.signIn` and read the session back with `resolveSession`.
* Catch an `AuthError` and read its code.

## The moving parts

<MermaidDiagram
  chart={`flowchart LR
  R["request carrying a cookie"] --> T["transport: finds the sid"]
  T --> E["AuthEngine"]
  P["provider: password"] --> E
  E --> S["stores: identities, credentials, sessions"]
  E --> A["session + identity"]`}
/>

The engine holds no data of its own. A **store** keeps identities, credentials and sessions; a **transport** decides how the session id travels; a **provider** is one way to prove who you are. Swapping any of them later leaves the rest of the code alone.

## Step by step

<Steps>
<Step>Build the engine</Step>

```ts title="src/auth.ts"
import { MemoryAdapter } from '@gentleduck/auth/adapters/memory'
import { createAuth } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'
import { cookieTransport } from '@gentleduck/auth/core/transport'
import { passwords } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/passwords'

export const auth = createAuth({
  baseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
  stores: new MemoryAdapter(),
  transport: cookieTransport({ name: 'sid', secure: false }),
  providers: [passwords()],
})
```

* `MemoryAdapter` holds all three stores in maps, so a restart forgets everything. Chapter 8 replaces it with Postgres.
* `cookieTransport({ name: 'sid', secure: false })` puts the session id in a cookie that works over plain http. The default name, `__Host-duck-sid`, needs https.
* `passwords()` hashes with Argon2id through the `@node-rs/argon2` peer.
* `baseUrl` is where the app lives. Links the engine mails start from it.

<Step>Sign in</Step>

```ts title="src/main.ts"
import { AuthError } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'
import { auth } from './auth'

const ada = await auth.identities.create({ profile: { username: 'ada', email: 'ada@example.com' } })
await auth.passwords.set(ada.id, 'correct-horse-battery', auth.cfg.stores.credentials)

const { sid, session } = await auth.flows.signIn({
  providerId: 'password',
  input: { email: 'ada@example.com', password: 'correct-horse-battery' },
})
console.log('signed in at AAL', session?.aal)
// signed in at AAL 1

const request = { headers: new Headers({ cookie: `sid=${sid}` }) }
const resolved = await auth.resolveSession(request).orNull()
console.log('resolved', resolved?.identity?.profile.username)
// resolved ada

try {
  await auth.flows.signIn({ providerId: 'password', input: { email: 'ada@example.com', password: 'wrong-password' } })
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof AuthError) console.log('refused', err.code)
  // refused AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS
}

await auth.flows.signOut(sid)
console.log('after sign-out', await auth.resolveSession(request).orNull())
// after sign-out null
```

<Step>Run it</Step>

```bash
npx tsx src/main.ts
```
</Steps>

## What just happened

<MermaidDiagram
  chart={`sequenceDiagram
  participant M as main.ts
  participant F as auth.flows
  participant P as password provider
  participant S as sessions
  M->>F: signIn with email and password
  F->>P: complete
  P-->>F: Ada, factor password
  F->>S: mint a session
  S-->>F: row stored under the hash of the sid
  F-->>M: sid, session, intents`}
/>

1. **An identity is the person.** `identities.create` stores a profile holding at least `username` and `email`. The password is not on it: `passwords.set` stores a hash as a separate credential.
2. **The provider checks the password.** It finds Ada by email, case-folded and trimmed, and verifies the hash. A wrong password and an unknown email both throw `AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS`, and both run the hasher, so neither the answer nor its timing says which.
3. **The session is minted.** `sid` is a random id for the caller; the store keeps only its SHA-256 as the row id. `session.aal` is 1 because one factor was presented.
4. **`intents` are for a server.** They say "set the `sid` cookie and the `duck-csrf` cookie". With no server yet, this chapter drops them; chapter 4 applies them.
5. **`resolveSession` reads it back.** The transport finds `sid` in the `cookie` header, the engine hashes it, loads the row and its identity.
6. **`signOut` revokes the row.** The same cookie now reads as no session.

## Answers

`resolveSession` answers an `Answer`: awaited directly, a missing or dead session throws. `.orNull()` turns only "not found" codes into `null` and still throws a store that is down, so an outage never reads as a signed-out user.

```ts
await auth.resolveSession({ headers: new Headers() }) // throws AUTH_SESSION_REVOKED
await auth.resolveSession({ headers: new Headers() }).orNull() // null
```

Every error the engine throws is an `AuthError` with a `code`, an HTTP `status` and `meta`. Branch on the code; the [error reference](/duck-auth/core/errors) lists them.

## Try it

1. Sign in as `ghost@example.com`, which does not exist, and confirm the code is the same as for a wrong password.
2. Print `session.expiresAt` and `session.absoluteExpiresAt`: 7 and 30 days out. Chapter 3 changes them.
3. Replace `passwords()` with `passwords({ hasher: scryptHasher() })`, imported from the same module, and uninstall `@node-rs/argon2`. Sign-in still works on Node's built-in scrypt.

## Where we are

```
ducknotes/
  src/
    auth.ts   - the engine
    main.ts   - the script you run
```

## See also

* [Core](/duck-auth/core): every `createAuth` option and facet.
* [Password](/duck-auth/providers/password): the strength policy and the hashers.
* [Transports](/duck-auth/core/transports): cookie, bearer, JWT.
* [Chapter 2: accounts](/duck-auth/course/chapter-2)

content:
Ada now signs in from a laptop and a phone. This chapter looks at what each sign-in left behind, how long it lasts, and what happens when a cookie turns up somewhere it should not.

## Learning goals

* Read a session row and tell its two deadlines apart.
* Set the session lifetimes and a per-person cap.
* List a person's devices and sign out all but one.
* Configure hijack detection and carry out its reaction.

## Two sessions, one person

<MermaidDiagram
  chart={`flowchart LR
  ADA["Ada"] --> L["laptop session: Firefox, 203.0.113.7"]
  ADA --> P["phone session: Safari, 198.51.100.4"]
  L --> R1["row keyed by hash of sid"]
  P --> R2["row keyed by hash of sid"]`}
/>

Each sign-in is its own row, recording the IP and User-Agent it was issued to. The plaintext `sid` exists only in the caller's cookie; the store holds its SHA-256.

## Step by step

<Steps>
<Step>Set the deadlines and the hijack policy</Step>

```ts title="src/auth.ts"
import { MemoryAdapter } from '@gentleduck/auth/adapters/memory'
import { createAuth } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'
import { cookieTransport } from '@gentleduck/auth/core/transport'
import { passwords } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/passwords'
import { deliver } from './mailer'

export const auth = createAuth({
  baseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
  deliver,
  stores: new MemoryAdapter(),
  transport: cookieTransport({ name: 'sid', secure: false }),
  providers: [passwords()],
  session: {
    ttlMs: 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000,
    absoluteTtlMs: 14 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000,
    maxSessionsPerIdentity: 5,
  },
  hijack: { onIpChange: 'rotate', onUserAgentChange: 'revoke' },
})

auth.events.on('suspicious', ({ signal, score }) => console.log('suspicious', signal, score))
```

<Step>Two devices, then one</Step>

```ts title="src/main.ts"
import { AuthError } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'
import { auth } from './auth'

const ada = await auth.identities.create({ profile: { username: 'ada', email: 'ada@example.com' } })
await auth.passwords.set(ada.id, 'correct-horse-battery', auth.cfg.stores.credentials)
const input = { email: 'ada@example.com', password: 'correct-horse-battery' }

const phone = await auth.flows.signIn({ providerId: 'password', input, ip: '198.51.100.4', userAgent: 'Safari' })

// false  <tomorrow>  <in two weeks>

// [ 'Firefox from 203.0.113.7', 'Safari from 198.51.100.4' ]

console.log((await auth.sessions.listForIdentity(ada.id)).map((session) => session.userAgent))
```

<Step>A cookie somewhere it should not be</Step>

Add to `src/main.ts`:

```ts title="src/main.ts"

const resolved = await auth.resolveSession({ headers: cookie })

console.log(await auth.hijack.evaluate(resolved.session, { ip: '192.0.2.99', userAgent: 'Firefox' }))
// suspicious ip-change 0.6
// { ok: false, reaction: 'rotate', signal: 'ip-change', from: '203.0.113.7', to: '192.0.2.99' }

const drift = await auth.hijack.evaluate(resolved.session, { ip: '203.0.113.7', userAgent: 'curl/8.0' })
// suspicious user-agent-change 0.8
try {
  if (!drift.ok) await auth.hijack.applyReaction(drift.reaction, resolved.session)
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof AuthError) console.log('refused', err.code)
  // refused AUTH_SESSION_REVOKED
}
console.log('laptop', await auth.resolveSession({ headers: cookie }).orNull())
// laptop null
```
</Steps>

## What just happened

1. **The row id is not the sid.** `session.id` is the SHA-256 of `sid`, so a leaked session table holds nothing a browser can present.
2. **Two deadlines.** `expiresAt` is the idle one: a day here, slid forward by `resolveSession` once less than half of it is left. `absoluteExpiresAt` is fixed at creation, two weeks here, and nothing moves it. Past either, the session reads as gone.
3. **`revokeAllExcept` kept the laptop.** It is the "sign out other devices" button. The phone's cookie now resolves to `null`.
4. **An IP change answered `'rotate'`.** Networks change, so the default reaction is to re-issue the session, not to end it. `evaluate` only judges; performing a rotate is yours, through `auth.sessions.rotateOrCreate` with `purpose: 'drift'`.
5. **A User-Agent change answered `'revoke'`,** because this engine said so. `applyReaction` ended the session and threw `AUTH_SESSION_REVOKED`. The default for a User-Agent change is `'mfa'`, which throws `AUTH_STEP_UP_REQUIRED` instead.
6. **Every drift emitted `suspicious`,** whatever the reaction.

## Rotation

Every change to who a session belongs to, or how strongly it was proven, mints a new row and a new sid. A sid planted in a browser before sign-in never becomes a signed-in one.

<MermaidDiagram
  chart={`flowchart LR
  A["sid A: guest or stale"] --> S["signIn"]
  S --> B["sid B: new row"]
  S --> X["sid A revoked"]
  B --> U["step-up: chapter 7"]
  U --> C["sid C at AAL 2"]`}
/>

`flows.signIn` takes `previousSid`, the sid the request arrived with, and revokes it. The server adapters pass it for you from chapter 4 on.

## Try it

1. Sign Ada in six times. With `maxSessionsPerIdentity: 5`, the oldest session is revoked as the sixth is minted.
2. Change `onUserAgentChange` to `'ignore'` and rerun. `suspicious` still fires, `evaluate` answers `{ ok: true }`, and the laptop session survives.
3. Leave out the `userAgent` on the drifted request. The reaction softens from `'revoke'` to `'rotate'`, so a proxy stripping a header cannot revoke every session behind it. `onMissingSignal: 'strict'` turns that off.

```
    main.ts
```

content:
An account needs more than a password: a proven address, a way back in when the password is forgotten, and a record of what happened. All three go out by mail, and duck-auth sends no mail itself.

## Learning goals

* Write the `deliver` function every link goes through.
* Verify an email address with a mailed token.
* Reset a password without revealing which addresses have accounts.
* Subscribe to engine events.

## Where the links go

<MermaidDiagram
  chart={`flowchart LR
  F["auth.flows.request..."] --> T["mint a single-use token"]
  T --> D["deliver: kind, identity, vars.url"]
  D --> MAIL["your mailer"]
  MAIL --> U["the person clicks"]
  U --> C["auth.flows.complete... with the token"]`}
/>

The engine mints the token, builds `baseUrl + callbackPath + '?token=...'`, and hands it to `deliver`. What happens next is your mailer's business.

## Step by step

<Steps>
<Step>A mailer that records instead of sending</Step>

```ts title="src/mailer.ts"
import type { Deliver } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'

export const outbox: { to: string; kind: string; url: string }[] = []

export const deliver: Deliver = async ({ kind, identity, vars }) => {
  outbox.push({ to: identity.profile.email, kind, url: vars.url })
}
```

`kind` says which message this is, `identity` is the recipient's whole row, and `vars.url` is the finished link. A real one calls your mail provider here.

<Step>Hand it to the engine, and listen</Step>

```ts title="src/auth.ts"
import { MemoryAdapter } from '@gentleduck/auth/adapters/memory'
import { createAuth } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'
import { cookieTransport } from '@gentleduck/auth/core/transport'
import { passwords } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/passwords'
import { deliver } from './mailer'

export const auth = createAuth({
  baseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
  deliver,
  stores: new MemoryAdapter(),
  transport: cookieTransport({ name: 'sid', secure: false }),
  providers: [passwords()],
})

auth.events.on('signup.completed', ({ identity }) => console.log('welcome', identity.profile.username))
auth.events.on('signin.failed', ({ reason }) => console.log('sign-in failed:', reason))
```

<Step>Verify, sign in, forget, reset</Step>

```ts title="src/main.ts"
import { orNull } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'
import { auth } from './auth'
import { outbox } from './mailer'

const lastToken = () => new URL(outbox.at(-1)?.url ?? '').searchParams.get('token') ?? ''

const ada = await auth.identities.create({ profile: { username: 'ada', email: 'ada@example.com' } })
// welcome ada
await auth.passwords.set(ada.id, 'correct-horse-battery', auth.cfg.stores.credentials)

await auth.flows.requestEmailVerification({ identityId: ada.id })
const { identity } = await auth.flows.completeEmailVerification({ token: lastToken() })
console.log('verified', identity.emailVerified)
// verified true

const input = { email: 'ada@example.com', password: 'correct-horse-battery' }
const { sid } = await auth.flows.signIn({ providerId: 'password', input })

const findIdentityByEmail = (email: string) => orNull(auth.identities.getByEmail(email))
console.log(await auth.flows.requestPasswordReset({ input: { email: 'ada@example.com' }, findIdentityByEmail }))
// { ok: true }
console.log(await auth.flows.requestPasswordReset({ input: { email: 'nobody@example.com' }, findIdentityByEmail }))
// { ok: true }

await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 10))
console.log(outbox.map((message) => message.kind))
// [ 'email-verification', 'password-reset' ]

await auth.flows.completePasswordReset({ token: lastToken(), newPassword: 'staple-battery-horse' })
console.log('old session', await auth.resolveSession({ headers: new Headers({ cookie: `sid=${sid}` }) }).orNull())
// old session null

await auth.flows.signIn({ providerId: 'password', input }).catch(() => {})
// sign-in failed: invalid-credentials
```
</Steps>

## What just happened

1. **Creating Ada emitted `signup.completed`.** Listeners run after the write; a listener that throws is logged, never raised into the flow.
2. **Verification was a round trip.** `requestEmailVerification` minted a token, stored its hash, and called `deliver` with `kind: 'email-verification'`. `completeEmailVerification` spent the token and set `emailVerified`. A token works once.
3. **Both reset requests answered `{ ok: true }`.** The one for a stranger sent nothing, but did the same store work, so neither the answer nor its timing tells an attacker which addresses have accounts. That is also why the request does not wait for `deliver`, and why the script pauses before reading the outbox.
4. **Completing the reset revoked every session.** Whoever had the old password may have signed in with it, so Ada's session from before is gone.
5. **The old password failed.** The flow threw `AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS`, and `signin.failed` reported it. Its `reason` is for your logs, never for the person signing in.

## The messages

| `kind` | Sent by | Link lands on | Lives |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `email-verification` | `flows.requestEmailVerification` | `/auth/verify-email` | 30 min |
| `password-reset` | `flows.requestPasswordReset` | `/auth/reset-password` | 30 min |
| `magic-link` | the magic-link provider (chapter 6) | `/auth/magic-link/callback` | 10 min |
| `account-deletion` | `flows.requestAccountDeletion` | `/auth/delete-account` | 30 min |

Each flow takes `callbackPath` and `ttlMs` to change the defaults. The path is where your page lives; that page reads `token` from the URL and calls the matching `complete` flow.

## Try it

1. Call `completeEmailVerification` twice with the same token. The second throws `AUTH_RECOVERY_TOKEN_INVALID`.
2. Make `deliver` throw. `requestEmailVerification` still resolves, and `signin.failed` fires with `reason: 'deliver threw'`: a mailer outage is reported, not raised.
3. Subscribe to `recovery.password.completed` and log the `identityId`. That is the event an audit log wants.

## Where we are

```
ducknotes/
  src/
    mailer.ts - deliver, recording to an outbox
    auth.ts   - the engine, now with deliver and listeners
    main.ts
```

## See also

* [Delivery](/duck-auth/core/delivery): every message kind and its `vars`.
* [Flows](/duck-auth/core/flows): verification, reset and account deletion.
* [Events](/duck-auth/core/events): every event and its payload.
* [Chapter 3: sessions](/duck-auth/course/chapter-3)

content:
Everything DuckNotes knows lives in maps, so a restart forgets every account and a second instance sees none of them. This chapter moves it all out of the process, puts the development settings back to their defaults, and has the engine refuse to start while anything is still wrong.

## Learning goals

* Keep identities, credentials and sessions in Postgres, beside your own tables.
* Share the limiter, the events and the OAuth `state` through Valkey.
* Know what `strict()` refuses in production, and build the engine in the order it needs.
* Test a flow against an in-memory engine.

## Where everything lives

<MermaidDiagram
  chart={`flowchart LR
  A["instance 1"] --> PG["Postgres: identities, credentials, sessions, notes"]
  B["instance 2"] --> PG
  A --> V["Valkey: limiter, events, OAuth state"]
  B --> V`}
/>

## Step by step

<Steps>
<Step>Install the drivers</Step>

```bash
npm i drizzle-orm pg ioredis
npm i -D drizzle-kit @types/pg
```

Run Postgres and Valkey however you like. With Docker:

```bash
docker run -d --name ducknotes-pg -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=duck -p 5432:5432 postgres:17
docker run -d --name ducknotes-valkey -p 6379:6379 valkey/valkey:8
```

<Step>The engine</Step>

```ts title="src/auth.ts"
import { drizzlePgAdapter } from '@gentleduck/auth/adapters/drizzle/pg'
import { valkeyDPoPNonceStore, valkeyEvents } from '@gentleduck/auth/adapters/valkey'
import { createAuth, orNull } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'
import { cookieTransport } from '@gentleduck/auth/core/transport'
import { valkeyLimiter } from '@gentleduck/auth/limiters/valkey'
import { magicLink } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/magic-link'
import { mfaProvider } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/mfa'
import { github } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/oauth/github'
import { passwords } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/passwords'
import Redis from 'ioredis'
import { db } from './db'
import { deliver } from './mailer'

const stores = drizzlePgAdapter(db)
const redis = new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL ?? '')

export const auth = createAuth({
  baseUrl: 'https://notes.example.com',
  deliver,
  stores,
  limiter: valkeyLimiter({ redis }),
  events: valkeyEvents({ cmd: redis, sub: new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL ?? '') }),
  transport: cookieTransport(),
  providers: [
    passwords(),
    mfaProvider({ issuer: 'DuckNotes' }),
    (_engine, send) =>
      magicLink({
        callbackPath: '/magic-link',
        deliver: send,
        findIdentityByEmail: (email) => orNull(stores.identities.find({ email })),
      }),
    github({
      clientId: process.env.GITHUB_CLIENT_ID ?? '',
      clientSecret: process.env.GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET ?? '',
      redirectUri: 'https://notes.example.com/auth/providers/oauth:github/callback',
      stateSigningSecret: process.env.OAUTH_STATE_SECRET ?? '',
      nonceStore: valkeyDPoPNonceStore({ redis, prefix: 'auth:oauth:nonce' }),
      profileToIdentityProfile: (p) => (p.email ? { email: p.email, username: `github:${p.sub}` } : null),
      onFederationConflict: 'link-if-verified',
    }),
  ],
  strict: false,
})

auth.events.on('lockout', ({ identityId, until }) => {
  console.warn(`locked out ${identityId} until ${new Date(until).toISOString()}`)
})

auth.strict({ env: 'production' })
```

* `drizzlePgAdapter(db)` holds all three stores on your own connection, so the accounts and the notes share one database.
* `valkeyEvents` takes a second connection for `sub`, because a subscribed connection can run no other command.
* `cookieTransport()` with no options names the cookie `__Host-duck-sid`, a prefix browsers accept only on a Secure cookie that no other subdomain can set. The GitHub `stateCookie` goes back to its default, `__Host-duck-oauth`, the same way.
* The last three statements are in that order on purpose; see [The order](#the-order).

```ts title="src/server.ts"
  res.json(mine.map((note) => note.text))
})

app.post('/api/notes', async (req, res) => {
  await db.insert(notes).values({ identityId: res.locals.identity.id, text: String(req.body.text) })
  res.status(201).end()
})
```

and in `DELETE /api/notes`:

```ts title="src/server.ts"
  await db.delete(notes).where(eq(notes.identityId, res.locals.identity.id))
```

<Step>The pages</Step>

Drop `csrfCookieName` from both clients in `src/page.ts` and `src/magic-link.ts`. Over https the CSRF cookie is `__Host-duck-csrf`, which is the client's default, and the notes request reads it under that name:


```bash

NODE_ENV=production npx tsx src/server.ts
```

Deploy it behind https at the `baseUrl`, and change the GitHub app's callback URL to match. Replace the mailer too: `src/mailer.ts` still prints each link.
</Steps>

## What strict() refuses

Run chapter 7's engine with `NODE_ENV=production` and it stops at the first line that cannot work there: `memoryDPoPNonceStore()` refuses to be built. Past that, `strict()` throws one `AUTH_MISCONFIGURED` listing everything else at once:

| Chapter 7 had | Refused, because | Chapter 8 has |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The in-process nonce store | A `state` burnt on one instance replays on another. | `valkeyDPoPNonceStore` |
| No limiter | Each instance grants its own budget, so a fleet allows each guess once per instance. | `valkeyLimiter` |
| `MemoryAdapter` | A restart forgets it, and no other instance sees it. The error names each slot it fills. | `drizzlePgAdapter` |
| The in-process event bus | A lockout raised on one instance is never heard on another. | `valkeyEvents` |
| `secure: false` | The session cookie would travel over plain http. | `cookieTransport()` |
| `http://localhost:3000` | Links and callbacks would go out over plain http. | an `https` `baseUrl` |
| No `lockout` listener | Nobody hears that an account is being guessed at. | the listener |

[Production hardening](/duck-auth/advanced/security) lists every check.

## The order

`createAuth` runs `strict()` as it returns, for the environment in `NODE_ENV`, and a `lockout` listener cannot exist before `createAuth` returns. So a production engine passes `strict: false`, subscribes, then calls `auth.strict({ env: 'production' })`. It throws while `src/server.ts` is still importing `auth`, so a misconfigured deploy never serves a request.

## Testing sign-in

```bash
npm i -D vitest
```

```ts title="test/sign-in.test.ts"
import { AuthError } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'
import { MemoryLimiter } from '@gentleduck/auth/limiters/memory'
import { createTest } from '@gentleduck/auth/test'
import { expect, it } from 'vitest'

it('locks an account out after repeated wrong passwords', async () => {
  const auth = createTest({ limiter: new MemoryLimiter({ max: 2, windowMs: 60_000 }) })
  const ada = await auth.identities.create({ profile: { username: 'ada', email: 'ada@example.com' } })
  await auth.passwords.set(ada.id, 'correct-horse-battery', auth.cfg.stores.credentials)
  const lockouts: string[] = []
  auth.events.on('lockout', ({ identityId }) => {
    lockouts.push(identityId)
  })

  const attempt = () =>
    auth.flows
      .signIn({ providerId: 'password', input: { email: 'ada@example.com', password: 'wrong-password' } })
      .catch((err: unknown) => (err instanceof AuthError ? err.code : 'unexpected'))

  expect(await attempt()).toBe('AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS')
  expect(await attempt()).toBe('AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS')
  expect(await attempt()).toBe('AUTH_RATE_LIMITED')
  expect(lockouts).toEqual([ada.id])
})
```

```bash
npx vitest run
```

`createTest()` is an engine over a `MemoryAdapter` with the password and MFA providers, so a test needs no database. Its limiter allows 1000 attempts a minute; this one allows two, so the third wrong password is refused and `lockout` fires once.

## Try it

1. Remove the `lockout` listener and start the server. It refuses to start, naming the missing handler.
2. Sign in, stop the server and start it again. The session and the notes are still there. On `localhost`, curl sends the Secure cookies over plain http, so the calls from chapters 4 and 7 work with the token read from `__Host-duck-csrf`.
3. Delete Ada's row from `auth_identities`. Her credentials, sessions and notes go with it.

## Where we are

```
ducknotes/
  drizzle.config.ts
  public/
  src/
    db/
      schema.ts   - the auth tables and notes
      index.ts    - the connection
    mailer.ts
    auth.ts       - Postgres, Valkey, strict()
    server.ts     - notes in Postgres
    code.ts
    page.ts
    magic-link.ts
  test/
    sign-in.test.ts
```

* [Webhooks](/duck-auth/advanced/webhooks): events delivered to other services.
* [Multi-tenancy](/duck-auth/advanced/multi-tenancy): one engine for many tenants.
* [duck-iam bridge](/duck-auth/guides/iam-bridge): what each person may do, once you know who they are.

## See also

* [Drizzle](/duck-auth/adapters/drizzle): the tables, and the MySQL and SQLite adapters.
* [Redis and Valkey](/duck-auth/adapters/redis): moving sessions to Valkey too.
* [Production hardening](/duck-auth/advanced/security): every check `strict()` makes.
* [Testing](/duck-auth/advanced/testing): `createTest` and its overrides.

## Learning goals

content:
Every lifecycle change is published on `auth.events`: sign-ins, rotations, lockouts, MFA changes, impersonation. Subscribe for audit logs, alerts, cache busting, or [webhooks](/duck-auth/advanced/webhooks).

## Subscribing

```ts
const off = auth.events.on('lockout', async ({ identityId, until }) => {
  await pager.notify(`identity ${identityId} locked until ${new Date(until).toISOString()}`)
})

off() // unsubscribe
```

Payloads are typed per event name. Handlers run one after another; a handler that throws is logged and the rest still run, so a broken listener never fails the sign-in that emitted.

`strict({ env: 'production' })` refuses an engine with no `lockout` listener, since a lockout nobody hears is a brute force nobody sees.

## The events

| Event | Payload | Emitted when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `session.created` | `session`, `identity` | A session was minted. |
| `session.rotated` | `session`, `previousSessionId?` | A session was replaced through rotation. |
| `session.revoked` | `sessionId`, `identityId` | A session was deleted by request, cascade or rotation. |
| `session.expired` | `reason`, `sessionId?`, `identityId?`, `count?` | A session aged out: `'sliding'`, `'absolute'`, `'impersonation'` or `'gc'`. |
| `signin.success` | `identity`, `factors` | A sign-in issued its session. |
| `signin.failed` | `providerId`, `reason`, `ip?` | A sign-in, link or delivery failed. `reason` is for logs only. |
| `signup.completed` | `identity` | An identity was created. |
| `lockout` | `identityId`, `until` | The limiter refused an identity's attempt; `until` is epoch ms. |
| `mfa.enrolled`, `mfa.removed` | `identityId`, `method` | A second factor was added or removed. |
| `identity.linked` | `identityId`, `providerId` | A provider login was attached. |
| `identity.unlinked` | `identityId`, `providerId`, `allowedLockout` | A provider login was removed. |
| `identity.erased` | `identityId`, `reason` | An identity was erased for good. |
| `identity.impersonated` | `realIdentityId`, `targetIdentityId`, `reason`, `iamDecisionId?` | An impersonation began. |
| `identity.impersonation.ended` | `sessionId`, `realIdentityId`, `targetIdentityId`, `endedBy` | It ended: `'release'`, `'revoke'` or `'expiry'`. |
| `recovery.password.requested` | `identityId` | A reset link was sent. |
| `recovery.password.completed` | `identityId` | A password was reset through its link. |
| `recovery.mfa.escalated` | `identityId`, `credentialId` | A backup code stood in for the second factor. |
| `suspicious` | `signal`, `score`, `meta`, `identityId?` | Hijack or anomaly detection flagged a request. |
| `org.member.added`, `org.roles.set` | `orgId`, `identityId`, `roles` | A member joined an org, or their roles changed. |
| `org.member.removed` | `orgId`, `identityId` | A member left an org. |
| `authz.revoked` | `identityId`, `at` | Published by your authorization side; duck-auth only listens. |

`session.expired` is kept apart from `session.revoked` so an audit trail can tell "nobody did this" from "someone revoked this".

## The audit envelope

Every lifecycle change is published on `auth.events`: sign-ins, rotations, lockouts, MFA changes, impersonation. Subscribe for audit logs, alerts, cache busting, or [webhooks](/duck-auth/advanced/webhooks).

## Subscribing

```ts
const off = auth.events.on('lockout', async ({ identityId, until }) => {
  await pager.notify(`identity ${identityId} locked until ${new Date(until).toISOString()}`)
})

off() // unsubscribe
```

Payloads are typed per event name. Handlers run one after another; a handler that throws is logged and the rest still run, so a broken listener never fails the sign-in that emitted.

`strict({ env: 'production' })` refuses an engine with no `lockout` listener, since a lockout nobody hears is a brute force nobody sees.

## The events

| Event | Payload | Emitted when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `session.created` | `session`, `identity` | A session was minted. |
| `session.rotated` | `session`, `previousSessionId?` | A session was replaced through rotation. |
| `session.revoked` | `sessionId`, `identityId` | A session was deleted by request, cascade or rotation. |
| `session.expired` | `reason`, `sessionId?`, `identityId?`, `count?` | A session aged out: `'sliding'`, `'absolute'`, `'impersonation'` or `'gc'`. |
| `signin.success` | `identity`, `factors` | A sign-in issued its session. |
| `signin.failed` | `providerId`, `reason`, `ip?` | A sign-in, link or delivery failed. `reason` is for logs only. |
| `signup.completed` | `identity` | An identity was created. |
| `lockout` | `identityId`, `until` | The limiter refused an identity's attempt; `until` is epoch ms. |
| `mfa.enrolled`, `mfa.removed` | `identityId`, `method` | A second factor was added or removed. |
| `identity.linked` | `identityId`, `providerId` | A provider login was attached. |
| `identity.unlinked` | `identityId`, `providerId`, `allowedLockout` | A provider login was removed. |
| `identity.erased` | `identityId`, `reason` | An identity was erased for good. |
| `identity.impersonated` | `realIdentityId`, `targetIdentityId`, `reason`, `iamDecisionId?` | An impersonation began. |
| `identity.impersonation.ended` | `sessionId`, `realIdentityId`, `targetIdentityId`, `endedBy` | It ended: `'release'`, `'revoke'` or `'expiry'`. |
| `recovery.password.requested` | `identityId` | A reset link was sent. |
| `recovery.password.completed` | `identityId` | A password was reset through its link. |
| `recovery.mfa.escalated` | `identityId`, `credentialId` | A backup code stood in for the second factor. |
| `suspicious` | `signal`, `score`, `meta`, `identityId?` | Hijack or anomaly detection flagged a request. |
| `org.member.added`, `org.roles.set` | `orgId`, `identityId`, `roles` | A member joined an org, or their roles changed. |
| `org.member.removed` | `orgId`, `identityId` | A member left an org. |
| `authz.revoked` | `identityId`, `at` | Published by your authorization side; duck-auth only listens. |
