An identity is an account: one row with your profile fields, the provider logins linked to it, and whether its address was proven. `auth.identities` reads and writes it.

## The row

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | Generated by the store. |
| `profile` | Your fields. `email` and `username` are required and unique; everything else is yours. |
| `providers` | Linked logins, each `{ providerId, providerSub, addedAt, addedBy }`, such as `oauth:google` and Google's `sub`. |
| `emailVerified` | Whether the address was proven by a link or a verified IdP, not merely typed. |
| `version` | Optimistic-concurrency counter; `updateProfile` takes it and refuses a stale write. |
| `deletedAt` | Set by a soft delete; the row reads as absent while it is set. |
| `createdBy`, `updatedBy`, `deletedBy` | The actor each write was attributed to, or `null`. |

## Typing the profile

The profile type flows from the engine's first type parameter:

```ts
import { MemoryAdapter } from '@gentleduck/auth/adapters/memory'
import { createAuth } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'

type Profile = { email: string; username: string; name: string; locale?: string }

const auth = createAuth<Profile>({
  baseUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
  stores: new MemoryAdapter<Profile>(),
})

const ada = await auth.identities.create({ profile: { email: 'ada@example.com', username: 'ada', name: 'Ada' } })
ada.profile.name // string
```

The serialized profile is capped at 16 KiB by default; set `identities: { profileMaxBytes }` to change it, or `0` to remove the cap.

## Reading

```ts
await auth.identities.getById(id)
await auth.identities.getByEmail('ada@example.com').orNull()
await auth.identities.getByProviderSub('oauth:github', '583231').orNull()
```

Each answers an `Answer`: awaiting it throws `AUTH_IDENTITY_NOT_FOUND` for a missing or soft-deleted row, and `.orNull()` answers `null` instead. Email lookups are case-insensitive.

## Writing

```ts
const ada = await auth.identities.create({
  profile: { email: 'ada@example.com', username: 'ada', name: 'Ada' },
  emailVerified: false,
})

await auth.identities.updateProfile(ada.id, { name: 'Ada Lovelace' }, ada.version)
```

* `create` emits `signup.completed`, and refuses a taken email or username with `AUTH_EMAIL_TAKEN` or `AUTH_USERNAME_TAKEN`.
* Every write bumps `version`, a link included, so read the row again before an `updateProfile` that follows one.
* `updateProfile` merges the patch. A patch that changes `email` clears `emailVerified` in the same write, since a new address is unproven.
* `markEmailVerified(id, email)` sets the flag, and refuses once the identity no longer holds that address. `flows.completeEmailVerification` calls it for you.

## Provider links

```ts
await auth.identities.link(ada.id, { providerId: 'oauth:github', providerSub: '583231' })
await auth.identities.unlink(ada.id, 'oauth:github')
```

`link` refuses a provider the identity already holds, and a login another identity holds (`AUTH_PROVIDER_TAKEN`). `unlink` refuses to drop the last way in: the remaining links plus credentials such as a password must not reach zero. `flows.linkProvider` and `flows.unlinkProvider` wrap both for a signed-in user.

## Deleting

| Call | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `softDelete(id)` | Hides the row for the grace period (7 days by default, `identities.softDeleteGracePeriodMs`). |
| `restore(id)` | Clears a soft delete; after the window it throws `AUTH_GRACE_EXPIRED`. |
| `erase(id, { reason, operatorId })` | Removes the row and everything under it for good, and emits `identity.erased`. |
| `gc()` | Erases every row whose grace window has closed. Schedule it yourself. |

A soft delete does not end sessions; `flows.completeAccountDeletion` does both, and mails an undo link if asked.

## Bulk and export

```ts
const result = await auth.identities.bulkCreate(rows, { mode: 'skipExisting' })
// { created, skipped, failed }

const blob = await auth.identities.exportAll(ada.id, auth.cfg.stores.credentials, {}, { sessions: auth.cfg.stores.sessions })
// { identity, credentials, sessions, schemaVersion: '1', exportedAt }
```

`bulkCreate` matches existing rows by email: `skipExisting` passes over them, `merge` links the new logins onto them, `replace` erases and recreates them. `exportAll` is the GDPR right-of-access export, with every credential secret and session CSRF hash removed.

`softDeleteMany`, `restoreMany`, `eraseMany`, `updateProfileMany`, `linkMany` and `unlinkMany` do the same over a set.

A valid session can still arrive from somewhere it should not. `auth.anomaly` runs detectors over each request, combines what they notice into one score, and recommends `allow`, `step-up` or `deny`. It recommends only; the server adapters refuse a `deny`, and the rest is yours to act on.

Nothing is registered by default, and with no detectors the step is skipped entirely.

## Registering detectors

```ts
import { authMemoryDeviceFingerprintStore, deviceFingerprintDetector, sha256 } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'

auth.anomaly.register(deviceFingerprintDetector({ store: authMemoryDeviceFingerprintStore(), authSha256: sha256 }))
```

| Detector | Signal | Needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `deviceFingerprintDetector` | `new-device`, scoring 0.7, the first time an identity is seen on a device (`sha256` of the User-Agent and the IP's /24 or /48 network) | A store. The memory one is per process; implement `AuthDeviceFingerprint.IStore` over shared storage for a fleet. |
| `authImpossibleTravelDetector` | `impossible-travel`, when the distance from the last known position implies more than 900 km/h | `getLastSeen(identityId)`, answering a position you record, and `geo` on the request. |

A detector is any `{ id, evaluate(ctx) }` answering signals `{ kind, score, evidence }`, with `score` from 0 to 1.

## Running them

The detectors need the request, so they run only when `resolveSession` gets a `requestSnapshot`. The server adapters' actor wrappers pass one once you give them `getCaller`:

```ts
app.use(
  expressActorContext(auth, {
    getCaller: (req) => ({ ...expressCaller(req), geo: lookupGeo(req.ip) }),
    onAnomaly: async (result) => {
      // called for every decision but 'allow', in place of the default refusal
      if (result.decision === 'deny') throw new AuthError('AUTH_ANOMALY_DENIED', { score: result.score })
      throw new AuthError('AUTH_STEP_UP_REQUIRED', { challenge: result.signals })
    },
  }),
)
```

* Without `onAnomaly`, a `deny` is refused with `AUTH_ANOMALY_DENIED` (403) and a `step-up` is let through, since a new device alone reaches the step-up score and refusing it would demand MFA on every first visit.
* With `onAnomaly`, the decision is yours: throw to refuse, including for a `deny`.
* What a detector learns, such as a new device, is recorded only once the request is let through.

Calling `resolveSession({ headers }, { requestSnapshot })` yourself, branch on `result.anomaly?.decision` and call `result.anomaly?.admit()` once you serve the request.

## Scoring

Signals combine as `1 - (1 - a)(1 - b)...`, so more evidence always raises the score and it never passes 1.

| Setting | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `stepUpAt` | 0.7 | At or above: `step-up`. |
| `denyAt` | 0.95 | At or above: `deny`. |
| `threshold` | 0.7 | Emits `suspicious` for an `allow` scoring this much; every other decision always emits. |
| `detectorTimeoutMs` | 1000 | A detector slower than this is dropped for the request. |
| `reactions` | none | Per detector id, then signal kind (`'*'` for any detector): `'allow'` mutes the signal, `'step-up'` or `'deny'` forces at least that. |

```ts
createAuth({
  // ...
  anomaly: { denyAt: 0.9, reactions: { '*': { 'impossible-travel': 'deny' } } },
})
```

A detector that throws, times out or answers garbage is logged and skipped, so a broken plugin never locks users out, and a broken detector looks like one that found nothing. Watch the logs.

duck-auth mints tokens but never sends them. Every outbound message goes through one function you pass as `deliver`, so the transport (SMTP, Resend, SES, an SMS gateway, a queue) is whatever your app already uses.

## The contract

```ts
import type { Deliver } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'

const deliver: Deliver = async ({ kind, identity, vars, tenant }) => {
  // kind:     which message this is
  // identity: the recipient's whole identity row
  // vars:     what the message needs, narrowed by kind
  // tenant:   the tenant the flow ran under
}
```

`vars.url` is the full link, already carrying its token, built as `baseUrl + callbackPath + '?token=...'`. `vars.ttlMin` is how long it stays good.

| `kind` | Sent by | Extra `vars` | Default path, TTL |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `magic-link` | The magic-link provider's `begin` | none | `/auth/magic-link/callback`, 10 min |
| `password-reset` | `flows.requestPasswordReset` | `requiresMfa` | `/auth/reset-password`, 30 min |
| `email-verification` | `flows.requestEmailVerification` | none | `/auth/verify-email`, 30 min |
| `account-deletion` | `flows.requestAccountDeletion` | none | `/auth/delete-account`, 30 min |
| `account-deletion-cancel` | `flows.completeAccountDeletion` with `sendUndoLink: true` | `restorableUntil` (epoch ms) | `/auth/cancel-deletion`, the grace window |

Each flow takes a `callbackPath` and a `ttlMs` to override the default; the magic-link provider takes them as options. The path must be same-origin (it starts with `/` and has no `//`): a flow replaces one that is not with its default, and the magic-link provider refuses one at construction.

`requiresMfa` is true when the account has TOTP or WebAuthn MFA enrolled. Completing that reset then needs a stepped-up session of the same account, so the mail can say so.

## Wiring it

Pass `deliver` to `createAuth`. The flows read it from there. The magic-link provider takes its own `deliver`, so register it as a thunk to receive the engine's:

```ts

import { createAuth, type Deliver, orNull } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'
import { magicLink } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/magic-link'

const stores = new MemoryAdapter()

const deliver: Deliver = async (message) => {
  switch (message.kind) {
    case 'password-reset':
      return sendMail(message.identity.profile.email, 'Reset your password', message.vars.url)
    case 'magic-link':
      return sendMail(message.identity.profile.email, 'Your sign-in link', message.vars.url)
    default:
      return sendMail(message.identity.profile.email, 'Confirm it is you', message.vars.url)
  }
}

const auth = createAuth({
  baseUrl: 'https://app.example.com',
  deliver,
  stores,
  providers: [

  ],

declare function sendMail(to: string, subject: string, url: string): Promise<void>
```

## Failure and timing

* **Reset and magic-link requests do not wait for `deliver`.** Both take an email address from a stranger, and awaiting the mailer would make the answer slower for an address that exists. The answer is `{ ok: true }` either way and the message goes out behind it. The verification and deletion flows run for a known identity and await it.
* **A throw is reported, not raised.** duck-auth emits `signin.failed` with `reason: 'deliver threw'` and the message kind as `providerId`. It never reads the thrown error, since a mailer's error text tends to carry the recipient and the link.
* **No `deliver` is a misconfiguration.** A flow that needs one throws `AUTH_MISCONFIGURED`, and under `strict({ env: 'production' })` a magic-link provider without one fails at boot.
* **An unknown address sends nothing.** `requestPasswordReset` and the magic-link `begin` answer the same for a stranger as for an account, and do the same store work, so neither the body nor the timing tells them apart.

## Testing

`authTestDeliver()` from `@gentleduck/auth/test` records messages instead of sending them:

```ts
import { MemoryAdapter } from '@gentleduck/auth/adapters/memory'
import { createAuth } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'
import { passwords } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/passwords'
import { authTestDeliver } from '@gentleduck/auth/test'

const { deliver, outbox } = authTestDeliver()
const auth = createAuth({ baseUrl: 'http://localhost', deliver, stores: new MemoryAdapter(), providers: [passwords()] })

const ada = await auth.identities.create({ profile: { email: 'ada@example.com', username: 'ada' } })
await auth.flows.requestEmailVerification({ identityId: ada.id })
outbox[0]?.vars.url // 'http://localhost/auth/verify-email?token=...'
```

See [Testing](/duck-auth/advanced/testing).

duck-auth mints tokens but never sends them. Every outbound message goes through one function you pass as `deliver`, so the transport (SMTP, Resend, SES, an SMS gateway, a queue) is whatever your app already uses.

## The contract

```ts
import type { Deliver } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'

const deliver: Deliver = async ({ kind, identity, vars, tenant }) => {
  // kind:     which message this is
  // identity: the recipient's whole identity row
  // vars:     what the message needs, narrowed by kind
  // tenant:   the tenant the flow ran under
}
```

`vars.url` is the full link, already carrying its token, built as `baseUrl + callbackPath + '?token=...'`. `vars.ttlMin` is how long it stays good.

| `kind` | Sent by | Extra `vars` | Default path, TTL |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `magic-link` | The magic-link provider's `begin` | none | `/auth/magic-link/callback`, 10 min |
| `password-reset` | `flows.requestPasswordReset` | `requiresMfa` | `/auth/reset-password`, 30 min |
| `email-verification` | `flows.requestEmailVerification` | none | `/auth/verify-email`, 30 min |
| `account-deletion` | `flows.requestAccountDeletion` | none | `/auth/delete-account`, 30 min |
| `account-deletion-cancel` | `flows.completeAccountDeletion` with `sendUndoLink: true` | `restorableUntil` (epoch ms) | `/auth/cancel-deletion`, the grace window |

Each flow takes a `callbackPath` and a `ttlMs` to override the default; the magic-link provider takes them as options. The path must be same-origin (it starts with `/` and has no `//`): a flow replaces one that is not with its default, and the magic-link provider refuses one at construction.

content:
`auth.sessions` owns every session: flows, providers and step-up all mint and rotate through it. Most apps never call it to sign someone in (`flows.signIn` does that) and use it to list and revoke.

## The row

A session is stored under the sha-256 of its id; the plaintext `sid` only ever travels to the client.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | The hashed sid, the row key. |
| `identityId` | Who it belongs to; `null` for a guest. |
| `kind` | `'user'`, `'guest'`, or `'apikey'` for a machine signed in with an API key. |
| `aal` | Assurance level: 1 after one factor, 2 after a second. |
| `factors` | Every factor presented, each `{ method, completedAt }`. |
| `fresh` | Whether a factor was presented recently enough for a privileged operation. |
| `ip`, `userAgent`, `fingerprint` | Captured at creation and never refreshed; hijack detection compares against them. |
| `expiresAt`, `absoluteExpiresAt` | The idle deadline, and the hard cap set at creation. |
| `actingAs` | The operator and reason while an impersonation is open, else `null`. |
| `tenantId` | The tenant it was issued under; `null` is global. |

## Deadlines

```ts
createAuth({
  // ...
  session: {
    ttlMs: 7 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000, // idle deadline, the default
    absoluteTtlMs: 30 * 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000, // hard cap, the default
    freshnessMs: 5 * 60 * 1000, // how long a factor counts as fresh, the default
    maxSessionsPerIdentity: 10, // unset means unlimited
  },
})
```

* `resolveSession` slides `expiresAt` forward once less than half the idle window is left, never past `absoluteExpiresAt`.
* Nothing moves `absoluteExpiresAt`. Once it passes, the user signs in again.
* Over `maxSessionsPerIdentity`, a new sign-in revokes that identity's oldest session. Guests are not counted.

An expired session reads as `AUTH_SESSION_EXPIRED`, which `orNull()` answers as `null`. The row stays until a sweep removes it; schedule `auth.sessions.gc()` yourself.

## Rotation

Every change to who a session is, or how strongly it was proven, mints a new row and a new sid through `rotateOrCreate`. That makes session fixation impossible to forget: a sid planted before sign-in never becomes an authenticated one.

| Purpose | Raised by | The previous session |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `signin`, `re-auth`, `sign-up` | `flows.signIn`, `flows.completeSignUp` | revoked |
| `step-up` | `flows.completeStepUp` | kept, marked not fresh |
| `step-down`, `drift` | your code, the hijack `'rotate'` reaction | revoked |
| `credential-change` | a password reset or change | every session of the identity revoked |
| `guest-promotion` | `sessions.promoteGuest` | revoked |
| `impersonate-start`, `impersonate-release` | `flows.impersonate`, `flows.releaseImpersonation` | revoked |

A step-up keeps the old row so a second tab holding it still works, at its old level and never fresh.

## Reading and revoking

```ts
const devices = await auth.sessions.listForIdentity(identity.id) // live rows, no csrfHash
await auth.sessions.revoke(sid) // by plaintext sid; answers the row it removed
await auth.sessions.revokeByHash(session.id) // by row id, for a device list
await auth.sessions.revokeAllExcept(identity.id, currentSid) // "sign out other devices"
await auth.sessions.revokeAllForIdentity(identity.id) // everywhere
```

`revoke` and `revokeByHash` throw `AUTH_SESSION_REVOKED` for a session already gone; `.orNull()` reads a repeat as a no-op. `revokeAllExcept` revokes everything when `currentSid` matches nothing, rather than keep a session you did not mean to.

In a multi-tenant deployment pass the tenant (`{ tenantId }`) to `listForIdentity`, `revokeAllExcept` and `revokeAllForIdentity`; without it they reach every tenant's sessions.

## Minting by hand

`create` answers the row, the plaintext `sid` and the CSRF token; the transport turns them into response intents:

```ts
const { session, sid, csrfToken } = await auth.sessions.create({
  identityId: identity.id,
  kind: 'user',
  aal: 1,
  factors: [{ method: 'password', completedAt: new Date() }],
})
const intents = auth.transport.issue(sid, session, { fresh: true, absolute: false, csrfToken })
```

Prefer `flows.signIn`, which runs the provider's checks, records the caller's IP and User-Agent, revokes the sid the request came in on, and emits `signin.success`.

## Guests

A guest session names nobody, for a cart or a draft before sign-in:

```ts
const guest = await auth.sessions.createGuest({ ip, userAgent })

// later, once they sign in:
const promoted = await auth.sessions.promoteGuest({
  guestSid: guest.sid,
  identityId: identity.id,
  aal: 1,
  factors: [{ method: 'password', completedAt: new Date() }],
})
```

Promotion rotates the sid, so anything the guest owned must move by identity, not by session. `promoteGuest` refuses a sid that is not a guest's.

## Hijack detection

Each session records the IP and User-Agent it was issued to. When a later request arrives from somewhere else, `auth.hijack.evaluate(session, { ip, userAgent })` answers `{ ok: false, reaction, signal, from, to }`, or `{ ok: true }` when nothing drifted or the drift is ignored, and `auth.hijack.applyReaction(reaction, session)` carries it out:

| Reaction | Default for | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `'rotate'` | IP change | Yours to perform: re-issue with `rotateOrCreate({ purpose: 'drift' })`. |
| `'mfa'` | User-Agent change | Refuses with `AUTH_STEP_UP_REQUIRED`. |
| `'revoke'` | | Ends the session and refuses with `AUTH_SESSION_REVOKED`. |
| `'ignore'` | | Records the drift only. |

```ts
createAuth({
  // ...
  hijack: { onIpChange: 'rotate', onUserAgentChange: 'revoke', onMissingSignal: 'strict' },
})
```

Every drift emits `suspicious`, whatever the reaction. By default a request that omits a value the session recorded is softened to `'rotate'`, so a proxy stripping a header cannot revoke every session behind it; `onMissingSignal: 'strict'` applies the configured reaction in full.

The server adapters' actor wrappers run the check for you once you pass `getCaller`:

```ts
app.use(expressActorContext(auth, { getCaller: expressCaller }))
```

Without `getCaller` the baseline is recorded at sign-in and never compared.

})
```

Promotion rotates the sid, so anything the guest owned must move by identity, not by session. `promoteGuest` refuses a sid that is not a guest's.

## Hijack detection

Each session records the IP and User-Agent it was issued to. When a later request arrives from somewhere else, `auth.hijack.evaluate(session, { ip, userAgent })` answers `{ ok: false, reaction, signal, from, to }`, or `{ ok: true }` when nothing drifted or the drift is ignored, and `auth.hijack.applyReaction(reaction, session)` carries it out:

| Reaction | Default for | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `'rotate'` | IP change | Yours to perform: re-issue with `rotateOrCreate({ purpose: 'drift' })`. |
| `'mfa'` | User-Agent change | Refuses with `AUTH_STEP_UP_REQUIRED`. |
| `'revoke'` | | Ends the session and refuses with `AUTH_SESSION_REVOKED`. |
| `'ignore'` | | Records the drift only. |

```ts
createAuth({
  // ...
  hijack: { onIpChange: 'rotate', onUserAgentChange: 'revoke', onMissingSignal: 'strict' },
})
```

Every drift emits `suspicious`, whatever the reaction. By default a request that omits a value the session recorded is softened to `'rotate'`, so a proxy stripping a header cannot revoke every session behind it; `onMissingSignal: 'strict'` applies the configured reaction in full.

The server adapters' actor wrappers run the check for you once you pass `getCaller`:

```ts
app.use(expressActorContext(auth, { getCaller: expressCaller }))
```

Without `getCaller` the baseline is recorded at sign-in and never compared.

content:
Everything in duck-auth hangs off one `AuthEngine`. You build it once at boot and share it; it holds no per-request state.

## Building the engine

`createAuth()` is the entry point. It validates the config, builds the engine, and runs `strict()` for the environment.

```ts
import { MemoryAdapter } from '@gentleduck/auth/adapters/memory'
import { createAuth } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'
import { cookieTransport } from '@gentleduck/auth/core/transport'
import { passwords } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/passwords'

export const auth = createAuth({
  baseUrl: 'https://app.example.com',
  stores: new MemoryAdapter(),
  transport: cookieTransport(),
  providers: [passwords()],
})
```

| Key | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `baseUrl` | required | The public origin every link, redirect and callback is built against. Must be absolute http(s); a trailing slash is dropped. |
| `stores` | required | `identities`, `sessions` and `credentials`, plus an optional `orgs`. An adapter provides all of them; see [Adapters](/duck-auth/adapters). |
| `transport` | a secure `duck-sid` cookie | How the session travels. See [Transports](/duck-auth/core/transports). |
| `providers` | none | Providers, or thunks `(engine, deliver) => provider`. A falsy entry is skipped, so `cond && provider()` works. |
| `limiter` | `MemoryLimiter` | What every flow spends attempts against. See [Adapters](/duck-auth/adapters#limiters). |
| `deliver` | none | Your mailer. See [Delivery](/duck-auth/core/delivery). |

## Facets

| Facet | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `auth.flows` | The multi-step operations: sign-in, sign-out, step-up, password reset, email verification, sign-up, account deletion, impersonation, linking. See [Flows](/duck-auth/core/flows). |
| `auth.sessions` | Create, rotate, revoke and list sessions. See [Sessions](/duck-auth/core/sessions). |
| `auth.identities` | Accounts: create, update, link, soft-delete, erase, export. See [Identities](/duck-auth/core/identities). |
| `auth.providers` | The registry: `list()`, `has(id)`, `get(id)`. |
| `auth.passwords` | Strength checks and password writes. Needs `passwords()`. |
| `auth.mfa` | TOTP, backup codes, WebAuthn MFA, remembered devices. Needs `mfaProvider()`. |
| `auth.passkeys` | Passkey registration. Needs `passkey()`. |
| `auth.apiKeys` | Create, rotate and revoke API keys. Needs `apiKeyProvider()`. |
| `auth.orgs` | Organizations and memberships. Needs an `orgs` store. |
| `auth.hijack`, `auth.anomaly` | Session drift and risk scoring. |
| `auth.transport`, `auth.events`, `auth.limiter`, `auth.captcha` | What the config supplied, or the defaults. |
| `auth.plugins` | Plugins installed with `auth.use()`. |

A provider-backed getter throws `AUTH_PROVIDER_NOT_REGISTERED`, naming the factory to add, when its provider is missing.

## Resolving the caller

`resolveSession` reads the transport, looks the session up and loads its identity. It answers an [`Answer`](/duck-auth/core/errors#answers):

```ts
const resolved = await auth.resolveSession({ headers }).orNull()
if (!resolved?.identity) throw new AuthError('AUTH_UNAUTHENTICATED')
resolved.session.aal // 1, or 2 after a second factor
```

* `orNull()` answers `null` when the request carries no session or one that was revoked or expired.
* It still throws `AUTH_SESSION_IDENTITY_ERASED` when the session outlived its identity.
* `identity` is `null` for a guest session.
* Pass `{ expectedTenantId }` to refuse a session from another tenant, and `{ requestSnapshot }` to run the [anomaly detectors](/duck-auth/core/anomaly).

Reading a session slides its idle deadline once less than half of it is left, never past the absolute one.

## Transactions

`auth.withTransaction(tx)` returns a view whose stores run on your driver's transaction handle and whose events wait in `pending` until you publish them:

```ts
await db.transaction(async (tx) => {
  const bound = auth.withTransaction(tx)
  const ada = await bound.identities.create({ profile: { email: 'ada@example.com', username: 'ada' } })
  await bound.passwords.set(ada.id, 'correct-horse-battery', bound.stores.credentials)
  return bound.pending
}).then((pending) => pending.flush())
```

It throws `AUTH_MISCONFIGURED` when a store cannot join a transaction (the memory adapter, or a hand-mixed store bag).

## Plugins

A plugin bundles providers, event listeners, an install hook and a facet under one id:

```ts
await auth.use({
  id: 'audit',
  events: { 'signin.success': (p) => console.log('signed in', p.identity.id) },
})
```

Installing is all or nothing: a failure part-way unwinds what landed.

## Strict mode

`auth.strict({ env })` throws `AUTH_MISCONFIGURED`, listing every problem at once, when a production engine is holding something that only works in development: a memory store or limiter, an in-process event bus, an insecure cookie, a weak signing key, no `lockout` listener. `createAuth` calls it as it returns, before any listener can exist, so a production engine passes `strict: false` and calls `auth.strict({ env: 'production' })` once its `lockout` listener is subscribed. See [Production hardening](/duck-auth/advanced/security).

A composite runs several transports as one: it reads the credential from whichever the request used, and issues and revokes through all of them.

```ts
import { bearerTransport, compositeTransport, cookieTransport } from '@gentleduck/auth/core/transport'

createAuth({
  // ...
  transport: compositeTransport([cookieTransport(), bearerTransport()]),
})
```

A sign-in then sets the session and CSRF cookies and answers `{ token, expiresAt }` in the body, so a browser and a native app use the same endpoint.

* **Extract** asks every member. A request presenting two different credentials, such as a cookie for one user and a bearer for another, is refused with `AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS`, as RFC 6750 requires. `{ onMultipleCredentials: 'first' }` takes the first member's instead.
* **Verify** tries each member that can verify, and falls back to the session store when none vouches.
* **Issue and revoke** run through every member. Two members that both answer a JSON body, such as bearer and JWT, cannot be combined: a response has one body, so the first sign-in throws `AUTH_MISCONFIGURED`.

content:
The default transport. The session id rides in an HttpOnly cookie the page's JavaScript cannot read, and a second, readable cookie carries the CSRF token.

```ts
import { cookieTransport } from '@gentleduck/auth/core/transport'

createAuth({
  // ...
  transport: cookieTransport(),
})
```

Without a `transport`, `createAuth` uses `cookieTransport({ name: 'duck-sid' })`: the same cookie under a name without the `__Host-` prefix.

| Option | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `name` | `__Host-duck-sid`, or `duck-sid` with a `domain` | The `__Host-` prefix makes browsers insist on Secure, `Path=/` and no Domain. |
| `secure` | `true` | Set `false` only for plain-http local development; `strict()` refuses it in production. |
| `sameSite` | `'lax'` | `'none'` requires `secure`. |
| `path` | `/` | The `__Host-` prefix requires `/`. |
| `domain` | none | Shares the cookie across subdomains; forbidden with a `__Host-` name. |
| `maxAgeSec` | the session's absolute deadline | Ends the cookie earlier than the session. |

A contradiction, such as a `__Host-` name with a `domain`, throws `AUTH_MISCONFIGURED` at construction.

## The CSRF cookie

Every sign-in also sets `__Host-duck-csrf` (or `duck-csrf` when the settings rule out the prefix) with the session's CSRF token. It is not HttpOnly: the client reads it and echoes it in the `x-csrf-token` header on every state-changing request. The server adapters check it; a mismatch answers 403 `AUTH_CSRF`. The duck-auth clients do this for you.

`transport.csrfCookieName` answers the name in use, for a client configured by hand.

## Local development

Browsers drop a Secure cookie over plain http on anything but `localhost`, and a `__Host-` name requires Secure. For http development pass a plain name:

```ts
cookieTransport({ name: 'sid', secure: false })
```

The CSRF cookie follows, becoming `duck-csrf`.

content:
A transport decides how the session id reaches the client and comes back. It reads the credential off a request (`extract`), writes it onto a response (`issue`, as intents), and clears it (`revoke`). The engine holds one, `createAuth({ transport })`, and defaults to a cookie.

| Transport | Carries | Revocation | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Cookie](/duck-auth/core/transports/cookie) | The sid in an HttpOnly cookie, plus a CSRF cookie | Immediate | Browser apps on your own domain. The default. |
| [Bearer](/duck-auth/core/transports/bearer) | The sid in `Authorization: Bearer` | Immediate | Native and mobile apps, CLIs, scripts. |
| [JWT](/duck-auth/core/transports/jwt) | A signed token the server verifies without a store read | When the token expires | Services that must not hit the session store per request. |
| [Composite](/duck-auth/core/transports/composite) | Several of the above at once | Per member | One backend serving a browser and a native app. |

[DPoP](/duck-auth/core/transports/dpop) is not a transport: it verifies proof-of-possession headers for a resource server that binds its tokens to a client key.

## How a request resolves

`auth.resolveSession({ headers })` asks the transport for the credential. When the transport can verify it on its own, as JWT does, that answer is used; otherwise the sid is hashed and looked up in the session store. A request without a credential reads as no session.

## Writing your own

A transport is any object with `extract`, `issue` and `revoke`, and optionally `verify` for self-contained tokens:

```ts
import type { Transport } from '@gentleduck/auth/core/transport'

const headerTransport: Transport.ITransport = {
  extract: (req) => req.headers.get('x-session-id'),
  issue: (sid, session) => [{ type: 'json', status: 200, body: { sid, expiresAt: session.expiresAt } }],
  revoke: () => [{ type: 'json', status: 200, body: { revoked: true } }],
}
```

`issue` answers intents rather than touching a response, so the same transport works under every [server adapter](/duck-auth/server).

The session id travels as `Authorization: Bearer <sid>`. Sign-in answers it in the JSON body, and the client stores and sends it.

```ts
import { bearerTransport } from '@gentleduck/auth/core/transport'

createAuth({
  // ...
  transport: bearerTransport(),
})
```

A sign-in answers `{ token, expiresAt }`; sign-out answers `{ revoked: true }` and the client forgets the token. The session is still a row in the store, so revoking it takes effect on the next request.

| Option | Default |
| --- | --- |
| `header` | `authorization` |
| `scheme` | `Bearer` |

The token is refused, reading as no session, when the scheme does not match, the header joins several values with commas, or the token is over 4 KB.

Bearer requests carry no ambient credential a third-party page could ride, so the CSRF check exempts a request that has a bearer header and no session cookie.

content:
The session is signed into a JWT. Requests carry it as `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>`, and `resolveSession` verifies it with no session-store read.

```ts
import { jwtTransport } from '@gentleduck/auth/core/transport'

const secret = process.env.JWT_SECRET ?? '' // an empty key throws at construction

const jwt = jwtTransport({
  signKey: { kid: '2026-09', key: secret },
  verifyKeys: [{ kid: '2026-09', key: secret }],
  issuer: 'https://app.example.com',
  refresh: {},
})

createAuth({ /* ... */ transport: jwt })
```

A sign-in answers `{ access_token, expires_in, token_type: 'Bearer' }`, and with `refresh` set, a refresh cookie.

## Revocation

The token is checked by signature alone, so **revoking the session does not revoke a token already issued**: it keeps working until `exp`. Keep `ttlMs` short (15 minutes by default) and put the long-lived state in the refresh cookie, which a revoke does end. Use the [cookie](/duck-auth/core/transports/cookie) or [bearer](/duck-auth/core/transports/bearer) transport where sign-out must be immediate.

## Options

| Option | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `signKey` | required | `{ kid, alg?, key }`. `key` is the secret for HS256, a PEM private key otherwise. |
| `verifyKeys` | required | Every key a token may be signed with, `signKey` included, each `{ kid, alg?, key, notAfter? }`. |
| `issuer` | required | Written as `iss` and required on verify. |
| `audience` | none | Written as `aud` and required on verify when set. |
| `ttlMs` | 15 minutes | Never past the session's own deadlines. |
| `freshnessMs` | 5 minutes | How long after sign-in the rebuilt session counts as fresh. |
| `clockSkewSec` | 0 | Leeway on `exp` for servers whose clocks disagree. |
| `refresh` | off | `{ cookieName?, ttlMs?, sameSite? }`; cookie `__Host-duck-refresh`, 7 days, `'strict'`. |

`alg` is `HS256` (the default), `ES256`, `RS256` or `EdDSA`, and a token is refused unless its header names the alg pinned to its `kid`. `strict()` refuses an HS256 secret under 32 bytes in production.

The token carries the session's `ip` and `userAgent` for hijack detection. Anyone holding it can read them.

## Refreshing

The refresh cookie holds the plaintext session id. Your refresh route reads it, checks the session is still live, and mints a new access token without rotating:

```ts

The session is signed into a JWT. Requests carry it as `Authorization: Bearer <jwt>`, and `resolveSession` verifies it with no session-store read.

```ts
import { jwtTransport } from '@gentleduck/auth/core/transport'

const secret = process.env.JWT_SECRET ?? '' // an empty key throws at construction

const jwt = jwtTransport({
  signKey: { kid: '2026-09', key: secret },
  verifyKeys: [{ kid: '2026-09', key: secret }],
  issuer: 'https://app.example.com',
  refresh: {},
})

createAuth({ /* ... */ transport: jwt })
```

A sign-in answers `{ access_token, expires_in, token_type: 'Bearer' }`, and with `refresh` set, a refresh cookie.

## Revocation

The token is checked by signature alone, so **revoking the session does not revoke a token already issued**: it keeps working until `exp`. Use the [cookie](/duck-auth/core/transports/cookie) or [bearer](/duck-auth/core/transports/bearer) transport where sign-out must be immediate.

## Options

| Option | Default | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `signKey` | required | `{ kid, alg?, key }`. `key` is the secret for HS256, a PEM private key otherwise. |

| `audience` | none | Written as `aud` and required on verify when set. |
| `ttlMs` | 15 minutes | Never past the session's own deadlines. |
| `freshnessMs` | 5 minutes | How long after sign-in the rebuilt session counts as fresh. |
| `clockSkewSec` | 0 | Leeway on `exp` for servers whose clocks disagree. |

DPoP binds a token to a key pair the client holds. Each request carries a `DPoP` header: a short JWT, signed with the client's private key, naming the method and URL. `DPoPVerifier` checks one.

It is a building block for your own resource server, not a transport: the built-in transports do not bind their tokens to a key. Your token issuer puts the key's thumbprint in the token as `cnf.jkt` (`bindPayloadToDPoP(payload, jkt)` does that), and each request's proof must match it.

```ts
import { dPoPVerifier } from '@gentleduck/auth/core/transport'
import { redisDPoPNonceStore } from '@gentleduck/auth/adapters/redis'

const dpop = dPoPVerifier({ nonceStore: redisDPoPNonceStore({ redis }) })

const { jkt } = await dpop.verify(request.headers.get('dpop') ?? '', { method: request.method, url: request.url }, accessToken)
if (jkt !== token.cnf.jkt) throw new AuthError('AUTH_DPOP_INVALID', { reason: 'key mismatch' })
```

`verify` checks the signature, that the proof's key fits its algorithm, the method and URL, the age of the proof, the `ath` hash of the access token when one is passed, and that its `jti` was not seen before. Any failure throws `AUTH_DPOP_INVALID`.

| Option | Default |
| --- | --- |
| `acceptedAlgs` | `['ES256', 'EdDSA']`; `RS256` and `PS256` can be added |
| `freshnessMs` | 60 seconds |
| `clockSkewMs` | 30 seconds |
| `nonceStore` | in memory; use `redisDPoPNonceStore` or `valkeyDPoPNonceStore` across instances |
| `expectedNonce` | none; a string or a function answering the server nonce the proof must carry |

The in-memory `jti` store only sees its own instance, so across a fleet a proof could be replayed against another one.

`@gentleduck/auth/core/dataAtRest` encrypts one field at a time, for values such as a national id or a date of birth that should never sit in the database in plaintext. Nothing in the engine or the stores calls it: you encrypt before writing the profile and decrypt after reading it.

```ts
import { authAesGcmDataAtRest } from '@gentleduck/auth/core/dataAtRest'

const dataAtRest = authAesGcmDataAtRest({
  kid: 'k1',
  masterKey: Buffer.from(process.env.PROFILE_KEY_K1 ?? '', 'base64'),
})

const ssn = await dataAtRest.encrypt('123-45-6789', { identityId: ada.id, field: 'ssn' })
const updated = await auth.identities.updateProfile(ada.id, { ssn }, ada.version)

const plain = await dataAtRest.decrypt(updated.profile.ssn, { identityId: ada.id, field: 'ssn' })
```

The context is part of the key: a ciphertext decrypts only under the `identityId`, `field` and optional `tag` it was written with, so one copied onto another row or field fails with `AUTH_INVALID_PARAMETERS`. Use `tag` for a tenant or a row revision.

Both encryptors refuse a plaintext over 1 MiB.

## AES-256-GCM with your own key

`authAesGcmDataAtRest({ kid, masterKey, previousKeys? })` derives a key per identity and field from a 32-byte master key, and writes `aes-256-gcm.v3$<kid>$...`.

* `masterKey` must be at least 32 bytes, and `kid` a non-empty string without `$`; both are checked at construction.
* To rotate, make the new key current and move the old one to `previousKeys`. Old ciphertexts still decrypt, and `needsReEncrypt(cipher)` answers `true` for them until you re-encrypt.

```ts
const dataAtRest = authAesGcmDataAtRest({
  kid: 'k2',
  masterKey: process.env.PROFILE_KEY_K2 ?? '',
  previousKeys: [{ kid: 'k1', masterKey: process.env.PROFILE_KEY_K1 ?? '' }],
})
```

## KMS envelope

`authKmsEnvelopeDataAtRest({ kms })` asks the KMS for a fresh data key per value, encrypts locally with it, and stores the wrapped key beside the ciphertext. The master key never leaves the KMS, and the identity and field travel as the KMS encryption context, so the KMS itself refuses to unwrap a key for a different row.

```ts
import { KMSClient } from '@aws-sdk/client-kms'
import { authAwsKmsProvider, authKmsEnvelopeDataAtRest } from '@gentleduck/auth/core/dataAtRest'

const dataAtRest = authKmsEnvelopeDataAtRest({
  kms: authAwsKmsProvider({ keyId: 'alias/profile-fields', client: new KMSClient({ region: 'us-east-1' }) }),
})
```

`@aws-sdk/client-kms` is an optional peer, loaded on first use. For another KMS, implement `Kms.Provider`:

| Member | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | Names the provider in logs. |
| `generateDataKey(context)` | Answers `{ plaintext, ciphertext, keyId }`: a 32-byte key and its wrapped form. |
| `decryptDataKey(wrapped, context)` | Unwraps it, refusing a context other than the one it was generated under. |

The KMS rotates its own keys, so `needsReEncrypt` always answers `false` here.

## Compliance

The gdpr, hipaa and fips [presets](/duck-auth/core/compliance) require `dataAtRest`. The engine cannot see whether you encrypt anything, so you attest it in `strict({ compliance: { dataAtRest: true } })`.

content:
A preset is a floor. `createAuth({ compliance })` shortens the session lifetimes to it, and `strict()` refuses to run until the deployment shows it meets the rest. It certifies nothing; it catches configuration that contradicts the regime you named.

```ts
const auth = createAuth({
  // ...
  compliance: 'hipaa', // or a list, such as ['gdpr', 'soc2']
  providers: [passwords({ compliance: 'hipaa' }), mfaProvider({ compliance: 'hipaa' })],
  strict: false, // checked below, once the listeners exist
})

auth.events.on('lockout', alertOnLockout)
auth.strict({
  env: 'production',
  compliance: { auditLogRetained7y: true, baaCompliantChannel: true, dataAtRest: true, mailerChannel: true },
})
```

* A list composes by taking the stricter value of every field.
* The checks run in every env, not only production, and one error lists every gap.
* `strict: false` defers them: `createAuth` runs `strict()` as it returns, before you have subscribed anything, and it has no way to take your attestations.

## What each preset sets

| | gdpr | hipaa | soc2 | fips |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sliding session | 7 days | 1 hour | 7 days | 4 hours |
| Absolute session | 30 days | 8 hours | 30 days | 12 hours |
| Password minimum | 8 | 12 | 8 | 14 |
| API key bytes | 32 | 32 | 32 | 48 |
| Needs `mfaProvider()` | no | yes | no | yes |
| Checks | `dataAtRest`, `mailerChannel`, `exportAvailable`, `softDeleteEnabled` | `dataAtRest`, `mailerChannel`, `baaCompliantChannel`, `auditLogRetained7y` | `lockoutListener`, `limiterRequired`, `auditLogRetained7y` | `dataAtRest`, `mailerChannel`, `fipsValidatedHasher`, `webauthnAttestationDirect` |

The session lifetimes only ever shorten what you set. The password, backup-code and API key floors belong to the providers, so pass the same preset to `passwords({ compliance })`, `mfaProvider({ compliance })` and `apiKeyProvider({ compliance })`; `createAuth` cannot reach providers that are already built.

hipaa and fips refuse an engine with no mfa provider. Sign-in still answers AAL 1; demanding the second factor is your `checkStepUp`, as in [step-up](/duck-auth/core/flows#step-up).

## The checks

| Check | Answered by |
| --- | --- |
| `limiterRequired` | The engine: a limiter you supplied that is neither the noop nor an in-process one. |
| `lockoutListener` | The engine: a `lockout` listener is subscribed when `strict()` runs. |
| `webauthnAttestationDirect` | The engine, when a passkey provider is registered. Otherwise you. |
| `fipsValidatedHasher` | The engine, from a shipped password hasher. A hasher of your own: you. |
| `dataAtRest`, `mailerChannel`, `baaCompliantChannel`, `auditLogRetained7y`, `exportAvailable`, `softDeleteEnabled` | You, in `strict({ compliance })`. |

What the engine sees overrides what you attest, so `limiterRequired: true` over a `MemoryLimiter` still fails. A check nobody answers fails.

content:
duck-auth throws one class, `AuthError`. Each carries a `code`, the HTTP `status` that code maps to, and a typed `meta`.

## AuthError

```ts
import { AuthError } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'

try {
  await auth.flows.signIn({ providerId: 'password', input })
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof AuthError && err.code === 'AUTH_RATE_LIMITED') {
    err.status // 429
    err.meta.retryAfter // seconds, typed from the code
  }
  throw err
}
```

`err.message` is the bare code. Anything a code needs to say rides on `meta`, typed per code, so `toThrow(/detail/)` in a test never matches; assert on `err.meta` instead.

`asAuthError(err, fallbackCode)` from `@gentleduck/auth/core/errors` passes an `AuthError` through and wraps anything else under the fallback, with the original on `cause`.

## Answers

Calls that look something up answer an `Answer`: a promise that throws when awaited, with readers that take the failure as a value.

```ts
const identity = await auth.identities.getByEmail(email) // throws AUTH_IDENTITY_NOT_FOUND
const maybe = await auth.identities.getByEmail(email).orNull() // null when there is no row
const named = await auth.identities.getByEmail(email).orDefault(guest) // guest when there is no row
const { data, error } = await auth.identities.getByEmail(email).wrap() // never throws
```

`orNull` and `orDefault` absorb only the codes that mean "no row", and rethrow everything else, so a database that is down never reads as a free email address:

`AUTH_CREDENTIAL_NOT_FOUND`, `AUTH_IDEMPOTENCY_MISS`, `AUTH_IDENTITY_NOT_FOUND`, `AUTH_IMPERSONATE_WINDOW_CLOSED`, `AUTH_JWT_INVALID`, `AUTH_JWT_KEY_UNKNOWN`, `AUTH_MEMBERSHIP_NOT_FOUND`, `AUTH_ORG_NOT_FOUND`, `AUTH_SESSION_EXPIRED`, `AUTH_SESSION_REVOKED`.

The set is exported as `ABSENT`. A few codes stay out of it on purpose: `AUTH_SESSION_IDENTITY_ERASED`, `AUTH_ANOMALY_DENIED` and `AUTH_TENANT_SCOPE_VIOLATION` are refusals or integrity failures, and must not quietly become an anonymous request.

`orNull(promise)` does the same for a plain promise, such as a store call:

```ts
import { orNull } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'

const findIdentityByEmail = (email: string) => orNull(stores.identities.find({ email }))
```

## On the wire

`errorToHttp(err)` from `@gentleduck/auth/server/generic` is what every server adapter answers with:

```ts
errorToHttp(new AuthError('AUTH_RATE_LIMITED', { retryAfter: 30 }))
// { status: 429, body: { ok: false, error: { code: 'AUTH_RATE_LIMITED', status: 429, retryAfter: 30 } } }
```

* An `AuthError` answers its status, with its meta spread into `error`. Meta keys that look like secrets are scrubbed.
* Anything else answers 500 with `detail: 'internal error'`, and is logged rather than described.
* The clients pass this body through untouched, so `result.error.code` in the browser is the server's code.

## Codes

| Code | Status | Raised when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AUTH_UNAUTHENTICATED` | 401 | No session where one is required, or its identity is gone. |

duck-auth throws one class, `AuthError`. Each carries a `code`, the HTTP `status` that code maps to, and a typed `meta`.

## AuthError

```ts
import { AuthError } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'

try {
  await auth.flows.signIn({ providerId: 'password', input })
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof AuthError && err.code === 'AUTH_RATE_LIMITED') {
    err.status // 429
    err.meta.retryAfter // seconds, typed from the code
  }
  throw err
}
```

`err.message` is the bare code. Anything a code needs to say rides on `meta`, typed per code, so `toThrow(/detail/)` in a test never matches; assert on `err.meta` instead.

`asAuthError(err, fallbackCode)` from `@gentleduck/auth/core/errors` passes an `AuthError` through and wraps anything else under the fallback, with the original on `cause`.

## Answers

Calls that look something up answer an `Answer`: a promise that throws when awaited, with readers that take the failure as a value.

```ts
const identity = await auth.identities.getByEmail(email) // throws AUTH_IDENTITY_NOT_FOUND
const maybe = await auth.identities.getByEmail(email).orNull() // null when there is no row
const named = await auth.identities.getByEmail(email).orDefault(guest) // guest when there is no row
const { data, error } = await auth.identities.getByEmail(email).wrap() // never throws
```

`orNull` and `orDefault` absorb only the codes that mean "no row", and rethrow everything else, so a database that is down never reads as a free email address:

`AUTH_CREDENTIAL_NOT_FOUND`, `AUTH_IDEMPOTENCY_MISS`, `AUTH_IDENTITY_NOT_FOUND`, `AUTH_IMPERSONATE_WINDOW_CLOSED`, `AUTH_JWT_INVALID`, `AUTH_JWT_KEY_UNKNOWN`, `AUTH_MEMBERSHIP_NOT_FOUND`, `AUTH_ORG_NOT_FOUND`, `AUTH_SESSION_EXPIRED`, `AUTH_SESSION_REVOKED`.

The set is exported as `ABSENT`. A few codes stay out of it on purpose: `AUTH_SESSION_IDENTITY_ERASED`, `AUTH_ANOMALY_DENIED` and `AUTH_TENANT_SCOPE_VIOLATION` are refusals or integrity failures, and must not quietly become an anonymous request.

`orNull(promise)` does the same for a plain promise, such as a store call:

```ts
import { orNull } from '@gentleduck/auth/core'

const findIdentityByEmail = (email: string) => orNull(stores.identities.find({ email }))
```

## On the wire

`errorToHttp(err)` from `@gentleduck/auth/server/generic` is what every server adapter answers with:

```ts
errorToHttp(new AuthError('AUTH_RATE_LIMITED', { retryAfter: 30 }))
// { status: 429, body: { ok: false, error: { code: 'AUTH_RATE_LIMITED', status: 429, retryAfter: 30 } } }
```

* An `AuthError` answers its status, with its meta spread into `error`. Meta keys that look like secrets are scrubbed.
* Anything else answers 500 with `detail: 'internal error'`, and is logged rather than described.
* The clients pass this body through untouched, so `result.error.code` in the browser is the server's code.

`auth.orgs` tracks which identities belong to which organizations, and the roles each holds there. The orgs themselves are yours: duck-auth reads them, and never creates, renames or deletes one.

## The store

Pass an `orgs` store next to the others: `stores: { ...drizzlePgAdapter(db), orgs: orgStore }`. `MemoryAdapter` ships one for tests, with `seedOrg(row)` to plant an org. In production you implement `Org.Store` from `@gentleduck/auth/core` over your own tables:

| Method | Must |
| --- | --- |
| `getOrg(id, ctx)` | Answer the org, or throw `AUTH_ORG_NOT_FOUND`. |
| `listOrgsForIdentity(identityId, ctx)` | Answer the orgs the identity is a live member of. |
| `listMembers(orgId, ctx)` | Answer the org's memberships. |
| `addMember(membership, ctx)` | Insert it, stamping `joinedAt`. |
| `removeMember(orgId, identityId, ctx)` | Set `leftAt`, or throw `AUTH_MEMBERSHIP_NOT_FOUND`. |
| `setRoles(orgId, identityId, roles, ctx)` | Replace the roles, or throw `AUTH_MEMBERSHIP_NOT_FOUND`. |

Every row carries a `tenantId` (`null` when global), and the facet refuses a row from a tenant other than the one asked for with `AUTH_TENANT_SCOPE_VIOLATION`. Without an `orgs` store, `auth.orgs` throws `AUTH_PROVIDER_NOT_REGISTERED`.

## Memberships

```ts
await auth.orgs.addMember({ orgId: 'acme', identityId: ada.id, roles: ['admin'] }, {})

const membership = await auth.orgs.resolveMembership('acme', ada.id, {}).orNull()
membership?.roles // ['admin']

await auth.orgs.setRoles('acme', ada.id, ['member'], {})
await auth.orgs.removeMember('acme', ada.id, {})

await auth.orgs.listForIdentity(ada.id, {}) // the orgs ada belongs to
await auth.orgs.listMembers('acme', {}) // live memberships only
```

* The last argument is the tenant context: `{}` for a single-tenant app, `{ tenantId }` otherwise.
* `addMember` refuses a live member with `AUTH_ALREADY_EXISTS`. Someone who left can be added again.
* `removeMember` marks the membership `leftAt` rather than deleting it; a left member stops appearing everywhere.
* Roles are deduplicated, empty or overlong entries are dropped, and at most 64 are kept.
* `resolveMembership`, `removeMember` and `setRoles` throw `AUTH_MEMBERSHIP_NOT_FOUND` for a non-member, which `.orNull()` reads as `null`.

Each write emits `org.member.added`, `org.member.removed` or `org.roles.set`.

## Roles and authorization

Org roles are labels duck-auth stores; it never decides what they allow. To enforce them, hand the membership to your authorization layer. With duck-iam, see the [IAM bridge](/duck-auth/guides/iam-bridge).

`auth.flows` runs the multi-step operations. Each one composes providers, sessions and identities, and answers the `intents` your server adapter applies to the response: cookies to set or clear, a redirect, a JSON body.

## Signing in and out

```ts
const { session, sid, intents } = await auth.flows.signIn({
  providerId: 'password',
  input: { email: 'ada@example.com', password: 'correct-horse-battery' },
  previousSid, // the sid the request arrived with, if any; it is revoked
  ip,
  userAgent,
})

const { intents: cleared } = await auth.flows.signOut(sid)
```

* `signIn` hands `input` to the provider's `complete`, mints the session through [rotation](/duck-auth/core/sessions#rotation), and emits `signin.success`.
* `session` is `null` and `sid` empty when the provider answered with something other than a session, such as an OAuth redirect.
* An unknown `providerId` throws `AUTH_PROVIDER_FAILED`.
* `signOut` revokes the session, ignores one already gone, and answers the intents that clear the transport.

`auth.flows.beginProvider(id, input)` runs a provider's first leg: the magic-link mail, the OAuth redirect, the passkey challenge.

## Step-up

Enrolling a second factor does not change sign-in, which still answers an AAL 1 session. A privileged route asks for more with `checkStepUp`:

```ts
const need = await auth.flows.checkStepUp(session, { aal: 2, methods: ['totp'], freshness: 5 * 60_000 })
if (!need.satisfied) {
  // need.reason: 'mfa-required' | 'fresh-required'; need.methods: what would satisfy it
}

const stepped = await auth.flows.completeStepUp({ currentSid: sid, method: 'totp', code, ip, userAgent })
stepped.session.aal // 2
```

`completeStepUp` takes `'totp'`, `'backup-code'`, or `'webauthn'` with a `webauthn` response, is rate limited per identity, and rotates to an AAL 2 session. A wrong code throws `AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS`. See [Adding MFA](/duck-auth/guides/mfa).

## Password reset

```ts
await auth.flows.requestPasswordReset({
  input: { email },
  findIdentityByEmail: (email) => orNull(auth.identities.getByEmail(email)),
})

await auth.flows.completePasswordReset({ token, newPassword })
```

* The request answers `{ ok: true }` whether or not the address exists, and mails a `password-reset` link through [Delivery](/duck-auth/core/delivery) when it does.
* Completing it spends the token, revokes every session of the account, then sets the password. A bad token throws `AUTH_RECOVERY_TOKEN_INVALID`, an old one `AUTH_RECOVERY_TOKEN_EXPIRED`.
* When the account has TOTP or WebAuthn MFA, a mailed link alone is not enough: it throws `AUTH_RECOVERY_REQUIRES_MFA` with the `methods`, until the call carries `currentSid` of a fresh AAL 2 session of the same account. That session is rotated rather than revoked, and its replacement comes back in `intents`.

## Email verification

```ts
await auth.flows.requestEmailVerification({ identityId: identity.id })
const { identity: verified } = await auth.flows.completeEmailVerification({ token })
verified.emailVerified // true
```

The request is rate limited per identity and does nothing for an address already verified, answering the same either way.

## Account deletion

Deletion is confirmed by mail, lands as a soft delete, and can be undone inside the grace window:

```ts
await auth.flows.requestAccountDeletion({ identityId: identity.id, reason: 'user asked' })

const deleted = await auth.flows.completeAccountDeletion({ token, sendUndoLink: true })
// deleted.restorableUntil, deleted.cancellationToken

await auth.flows.cancelAccountDeletion({ token: deleted.cancellationToken })
```

* `completeAccountDeletion` soft-deletes the identity and revokes its sessions. With `sendUndoLink` it mails an `account-deletion-cancel` link; without it, deliver `cancellationToken` yourself or drop it to turn undo off.
* `cancelAccountDeletion` takes either the undo token (the user's route) or `{ identityId, authorize }` (an operator's). Both or neither throws `AUTH_MISCONFIGURED`.
* Once the window closes, `identities.gc()` erases the row.

## Staged sign-up

For a sign-up that spans several screens, `beginSignUp` creates an unverified identity and answers a flow token the client keeps:

```ts
const { flowToken } = await auth.flows.beginSignUp({
  email: 'lin@example.com',
  required: ['email-verified', 'terms-accepted'], // the default
})

await auth.flows.advanceSignUp({ flowToken, stage: 'email-verified' })
await auth.flows.advanceSignUp({ flowToken, stage: 'terms-accepted', profilePatch: { username: 'lin' } })

const { session, intents } = await auth.flows.completeSignUp({ flowToken })
```

* Stages are `email-collected`, `email-verified`, `profile-completed`, `mfa-enrolled`, `terms-accepted` and `completed`. Your code proves each one before advancing it; `advanceSignUp` records it.
* `completeSignUp` throws `AUTH_SIGNUP_INCOMPLETE` with the `missing` stages, otherwise merges the collected profile and signs the user in.
* The flow expires 30 minutes after its last step and 24 hours after it began. A dead or spent token throws `AUTH_SIGNUP_TOKEN_INVALID`. `getSignUpFlow(flowToken)` reads the flow, and `.orNull()` answers `null` for a dead one.
* `profilePatch` cannot change the email the flow began with.

## Impersonation

Support staff can act as a user through a separate, audited session:

```ts
const acting = await auth.flows.impersonate({
  realSid: operatorSid,
  targetIdentityId: user.id,
  reason: 'ticket 4412',
  authorize: async (operator, targetId) => canImpersonate(operator.identityId, targetId),
})
acting.session.actingAs // { realIdentityId, reason, startedAt, expiresAt }

const back = await auth.flows.releaseImpersonation(acting.sid)
```

* `authorize` is mandatory and decides; with [duck-iam](/duck-auth/guides/iam-bridge) it wraps `engine.authorize()`. Never pass `async () => true`.
* The session lives at most an hour, emits `identity.impersonated`, and cannot impersonate again or target the operator.
* `releaseImpersonation` ends it and mints the operator a session of their own, or answers `session: null` when the operator's account went away meanwhile.

## Linking a provider

```ts
await auth.flows.linkProvider({
  identityId: identity.id,
  providerId: 'oauth:github',
  providerSub,
  authorize: async ({ identity }) => identity.id === signedInIdentityId,
})

await auth.flows.unlinkProvider({ identityId: identity.id, providerId: 'oauth:github' })
```

A link is a permanent way to sign in, so `authorize` must answer `false` unless `providerSub` came from a token exchange your own code performed. `unlinkProvider` refuses the last way in unless `allowLockout` is set, which is for deletion and admin overrides.

`auth.flows.beginProvider(id, input)` runs a provider's first leg: the magic-link mail, the OAuth redirect, the passkey challenge.

## Step-up

Enrolling a second factor does not change sign-in, which still answers an AAL 1 session. A privileged route asks for more with `checkStepUp`:

```ts
const need = await auth.flows.checkStepUp(session, { aal: 2, methods: ['totp'], freshness: 5 * 60_000 })
if (!need.satisfied) {
  // need.reason: 'mfa-required' | 'fresh-required'; need.methods: what would satisfy it
}

const stepped = await auth.flows.completeStepUp({ currentSid: sid, method: 'totp', code, ip, userAgent })
stepped.session.aal // 2
```

`completeStepUp` takes `'totp'`, `'backup-code'`, or `'webauthn'` with a `webauthn` response, is rate limited per identity, and rotates to an AAL 2 session. A wrong code throws `AUTH_INVALID_CREDENTIALS`. See [Adding MFA](/duck-auth/guides/mfa).

## Password reset

```ts
await auth.flows.requestPasswordReset({
  input: { email },
  findIdentityByEmail: (email) => orNull(auth.identities.getByEmail(email)),
})

await auth.flows.completePasswordReset({ token, newPassword })
```

* The request answers `{ ok: true }` whether or not the address exists, and mails a `password-reset` link through [Delivery](/duck-auth/core/delivery) when it does.
* Completing it spends the token, revokes every session of the account, then sets the password. A bad token throws `AUTH_RECOVERY_TOKEN_INVALID`, an old one `AUTH_RECOVERY_TOKEN_EXPIRED`.
* When the account has TOTP or WebAuthn MFA, a mailed link alone is not enough: it throws `AUTH_RECOVERY_REQUIRES_MFA` with the `methods`, until the call carries `currentSid` of a fresh AAL 2 session of the same account. That session is rotated rather than revoked, and its replacement comes back in `intents`.

## Email verification

```ts
await auth.flows.requestEmailVerification({ identityId: identity.id })
const { identity: verified } = await auth.flows.completeEmailVerification({ token })
verified.emailVerified // true
```

The request is rate limited per identity and does nothing for an address already verified, answering the same either way.

## Account deletion

Deletion is confirmed by mail, lands as a soft delete, and can be undone inside the grace window:

```ts
await auth.flows.requestAccountDeletion({ identityId: identity.id, reason: 'user asked' })

const deleted = await auth.flows.completeAccountDeletion({ token, sendUndoLink: true })
// deleted.restorableUntil, deleted.cancellationToken

await auth.flows.cancelAccountDeletion({ token: deleted.cancellationToken })
```

* `completeAccountDeletion` soft-deletes the identity and revokes its sessions. With `sendUndoLink` it mails an `account-deletion-cancel` link; without it, deliver `cancellationToken` yourself or drop it to turn undo off.
* `cancelAccountDeletion` takes either the undo token (the user's route) or `{ identityId, authorize }` (an operator's). Both or neither throws `AUTH_MISCONFIGURED`.
* Once the window closes, `identities.gc()` erases the row.

## Staged sign-up

For a sign-up that spans several screens, `beginSignUp` creates an unverified identity and answers a flow token the client keeps:

```ts
const { flowToken } = await auth.flows.beginSignUp({
  email: 'lin@example.com',
  required: ['email-verified', 'terms-accepted'], // the default
})

await auth.flows.advanceSignUp({ flowToken, stage: 'email-verified' })
await auth.flows.advanceSignUp({ flowToken, stage: 'terms-accepted', profilePatch: { username: 'lin' } })

const { session, intents } = await auth.flows.completeSignUp({ flowToken })
```

* Stages are `email-collected`, `email-verified`, `profile-completed`, `mfa-enrolled`, `terms-accepted` and `completed`. Your code proves each one before advancing it; `advanceSignUp` records it.
* `completeSignUp` throws `AUTH_SIGNUP_INCOMPLETE` with the `missing` stages, otherwise merges the collected profile and signs the user in.
* The flow expires 30 minutes after its last step and 24 hours after it began. A dead or spent token throws `AUTH_SIGNUP_TOKEN_INVALID`. `getSignUpFlow(flowToken)` reads the flow, and `.orNull()` answers `null` for a dead one.
* `profilePatch` cannot change the email the flow began with.

## Impersonation

Support staff can act as a user through a separate, audited session:

```ts
const acting = await auth.flows.impersonate({
  realSid: operatorSid,
  targetIdentityId: user.id,
  reason: 'ticket 4412',
  authorize: async (operator, targetId) => canImpersonate(operator.identityId, targetId),
})
acting.session.actingAs // { realIdentityId, reason, startedAt, expiresAt }

const back = await auth.flows.releaseImpersonation(acting.sid)
```

* `authorize` is mandatory and decides; with [duck-iam](/duck-auth/guides/iam-bridge) it wraps `engine.authorize()`. Never pass `async () => true`.
* The session lives at most an hour, emits `identity.impersonated`, and cannot impersonate again or target the operator.
* `releaseImpersonation` ends it and mints the operator a session of their own, or answers `session: null` when the operator's account went away meanwhile.

## Linking a provider

```ts
await auth.flows.linkProvider({
  identityId: identity.id,
  providerId: 'oauth:github',
  providerSub,
  authorize: async ({ identity }) => identity.id === signedInIdentityId,
})

await auth.flows.unlinkProvider({ identityId: identity.id, providerId: 'oauth:github' })
```

A link is a permanent way to sign in, so `authorize` must answer `false` unless `providerSub` came from a token exchange your own code performed. `unlinkProvider` refuses the last way in unless `allowLockout` is set, which is for deletion and admin overrides.

1. Register an application in the [Microsoft Entra admin center](https://entra.microsoft.com/).
2. Under **Authentication**, add a **Web** redirect URI: `https://app.example.com/auth/providers/oauth:microsoft/callback`.
3. Under **Certificates & secrets**, create a client secret, and note the **Application (client) ID**.

```ts
import { microsoft } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/oauth/microsoft'

microsoft({
  clientId: process.env.MICROSOFT_CLIENT_ID ?? '',
  clientSecret: process.env.MICROSOFT_CLIENT_SECRET ?? '',
  tenant: process.env.MICROSOFT_TENANT_ID, // default 'common'
  redirectUri: 'https://app.example.com/auth/providers/oauth:microsoft/callback',
  stateSigningSecret: process.env.OAUTH_STATE_SECRET ?? '',
  nonceStore,
  profileToIdentityProfile: (p) => (p.email ? { email: p.email, username: `microsoft:${p.sub}`, name: p.name } : null),
})
```

The provider id is `oauth:microsoft`, and the default scopes are `openid profile email User.Read`.

`tenant` picks who may sign in: `'common'` for any organization and personal accounts, `'organizations'`, `'consumers'`, or your directory's id to admit only your own.

The `email` Entra returns is set by each tenant's administrators and Microsoft documents it as unverified, so it is never marked verified. Under `'common'` anyone can create a tenant claiming any address. `'link-if-verified'` therefore never links a Microsoft sign-in to an existing account; link deliberately instead.

The routes, the options every provider shares and account linking are on the [OAuth](/duck-auth/providers/oauth) page.

1. Create an OAuth App under **Settings > Developer settings > OAuth Apps**.
2. Set **Authorization callback URL** to `https://app.example.com/auth/providers/oauth:github/callback`.
3. Copy the client id and generate a client secret.

```ts
import { github } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/oauth/github'

github({
  clientId: process.env.GITHUB_CLIENT_ID ?? '',
  clientSecret: process.env.GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET ?? '',
  redirectUri: 'https://app.example.com/auth/providers/oauth:github/callback',
  stateSigningSecret: process.env.OAUTH_STATE_SECRET ?? '',
  nonceStore,

* `sub` is the numeric account id as a string, which survives a username change.

content:
Each shipped provider is a preset over one OAuth 2.0 implementation: PKCE, a signed `state` bound to the browser that began the flow by a pre-auth cookie, and a callback that works once.

| Provider | Import | Default scopes | Email counted as verified |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Google](/duck-auth/providers/oauth/google) | `providers/oauth/google` | `openid email profile` | When Google says so. |
| [GitHub](/duck-auth/providers/oauth/github) | `providers/oauth/github` | `read:user user:email` | The primary verified address only. |
| [Microsoft](/duck-auth/providers/oauth/microsoft) | `providers/oauth/microsoft` | `openid profile email User.Read` | Never. |
| [Apple](/duck-auth/providers/oauth/apple) | `providers/oauth/apple` | `name email` | When the id\_token says so. |
| [LinkedIn](/duck-auth/providers/oauth/linkedin) | `providers/oauth/linkedin` | `openid profile email` | When LinkedIn says so. |
| [Discord](/duck-auth/providers/oauth/discord) | `providers/oauth/discord` | `identify email` | When Discord says so. |

## Setup

```ts
import { redisDPoPNonceStore } from '@gentleduck/auth/adapters/redis'
import { google } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/oauth/google'

const auth = createAuth({
  baseUrl: 'https://app.example.com',
  // ...
  providers: [
    google({
      clientId: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID ?? '',
      clientSecret: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET ?? '',
      redirectUri: 'https://app.example.com/auth/providers/oauth:google/callback',
      stateSigningSecret: process.env.OAUTH_STATE_SECRET ?? '',
      nonceStore: redisDPoPNonceStore({ redis, prefix: 'auth:oauth:nonce' }),
      profileToIdentityProfile: (p) => (p.email ? { email: p.email, username: `google:${p.sub}`, name: p.name } : null),
    }),
  ],
})
```

Every provider takes these, plus its own extras:

| Option | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `clientId`, `clientSecret` | From the IdP's console. Apple takes a key instead of a secret. |
| `redirectUri` | Must match what the IdP has registered, exactly. |
| `stateSigningSecret` | Signs the `state`. Empty throws; `strict()` refuses one under 32 bytes in production. |
| `nonceStore` | Burns each `state` on use, so a callback URL recovered from history or a log cannot sign in again. Required unless you pass `allowStateReplay: true`, which production refuses. `memoryDPoPNonceStore()` works for one process. |
| `profileToIdentityProfile` | Builds the profile for a first-time user. Without it, or when it answers `null`, a first sign-in is refused. |
| `onFederationConflict` | See [Linking](#linking-to-an-existing-account). Default `'reject'`. |
| `onSignIn` | Replaces the lookup below entirely. |
| `stateCookie` | The pre-auth cookie, `__Host-duck-oauth` by default. On plain-http development, pass `{ name: 'duck-oauth', secure: false }`. |
| `scopes` | Replaces the default scopes. |

## The routes

A flow is two requests: `begin`, which sets the pre-auth cookie and redirects to the IdP, and the callback the IdP sends the browser back to. With Express:

```ts
import { applyIntents, expressCaller, mountProviderBegin } from '@gentleduck/auth/server/express'
import { oauthCallback } from '@gentleduck/auth/server/generic'
import express from 'express'

app.post('/auth/providers/:id/begin', express.json(), mountProviderBegin(auth))

const callback: express.RequestHandler = async (req, res) => {
  const request = { body: req.body, cookie: req.headers.cookie, method: req.method, url: req.url }
  const intents = await oauthCallback(auth, req.params.id, request, expressCaller(req))
  applyIntents([...intents, { type: 'redirect', url: '/' }], res)
}
app.get('/auth/providers/:id/callback', callback)
app.post('/auth/providers/:id/callback', express.urlencoded({ extended: false }), callback)
```

* In the browser, `client.beginProvider('oauth:google')` posts to `begin` and follows the IdP URL it answers.
* The callback answers the session cookies and nothing else, so where the browser lands is yours: add the redirect, and on a thrown `AuthError`, redirect to your sign-in page with its code.
* The POST route is only for Apple, which posts its callback as a form.

The other [server adapters](/duck-auth/server) have the same pieces.

## Who signs in

On a callback, the provider finds the identity:

1. One already linked to this provider account signs in.
2. Otherwise, one owning the profile's email is a conflict, settled by `onFederationConflict`.
3. Otherwise, `profileToIdentityProfile` creates one, linked to the provider account.

A created identity starts with `emailVerified: false`: the IdP's claim is not a proof duck-auth made.

## Linking to an existing account

An existing account whose email matches is not linked by default. Linking on the IdP's word alone hands an account to anyone who can make an IdP assert its address.

| `onFederationConflict` | Links when |
| --- | --- |
| `'reject'` (default) | Never; the sign-in throws `AUTH_PROVIDER_FAILED`. |
| `'link-if-verified'` | The IdP marks the address verified and the existing identity proved it too. |
| `(conflict) => 'link' \| 'reject'` | Your function says `'link'`; anything else refuses. |

A signed-in user can link a provider deliberately with [`auth.flows.linkProvider`](/duck-auth/core/flows#linking-a-provider).

## Any other IdP

`oProvider` and `OAuthClient` from `@gentleduck/auth/providers/oauth/core` are what the six presets are built from:

```ts
import { getUserinfoString, OAuthClient, oProvider } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/oauth/core'

const gitlab = oProvider({
  providerId: 'gitlab',
  client: new OAuthClient({
    clientId: process.env.GITLAB_CLIENT_ID ?? '',
    clientSecret: process.env.GITLAB_CLIENT_SECRET ?? '',
    endpoints: {
      authorizationEndpoint: 'https://gitlab.com/oauth/authorize',
      tokenEndpoint: 'https://gitlab.com/oauth/token',
      userinfoEndpoint: 'https://gitlab.com/oauth/userinfo',
    },
    scopes: ['openid', 'email'],
  }),
  redirectUri: 'https://app.example.com/auth/providers/oauth:gitlab/callback',
  stateSigningSecret: process.env.OAUTH_STATE_SECRET ?? '',
  nonceStore,
  async fetchProfile(tokens, client) {
    const info = await client.userinfo(tokens.access_token)
    const sub = getUserinfoString(info, 'sub')
    if (!sub) throw new Error('gitlab userinfo carried no sub')
    return { sub, email: getUserinfoString(info, 'email') }
  },
})
```

`fetchProfile` answers `{ sub, email?, emailVerified?, name?, avatarUrl? }`. Set `emailVerified` only on a literal `true` from the IdP, since `'link-if-verified'` trusts it.

## Errors

| Code | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `AUTH_OAUTH_STATE_MISMATCH` | The `state` does not verify, is over ten minutes old, or reached a browser without the pre-auth cookie. |
| `AUTH_OAUTH_NONCE_REPLAY` | The callback was already used. |
| `AUTH_PROVIDER_FAILED` | The IdP refused the code, the profile had no subject, a conflict was refused, or `profileToIdentityProfile` answered `null`. |

When a sign-in is refused after the code was exchanged, the tokens are revoked at the IdP where it supports revocation.

1. Create an OAuth client of type **Web application** in the [Google Cloud Console](https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/credentials).
2. Add `https://app.example.com/auth/providers/oauth:google/callback` under **Authorized redirect URIs**.
3. Copy the client id and secret.

```ts
import { google } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/oauth/google'

google({
  clientId: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID ?? '',
  clientSecret: process.env.GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET ?? '',
  redirectUri: 'https://app.example.com/auth/providers/oauth:google/callback',
  stateSigningSecret: process.env.OAUTH_STATE_SECRET ?? '',
  nonceStore,
  profileToIdentityProfile: (p) => (p.email ? { email: p.email, username: `google:${p.sub}`, name: p.name } : null),
})
```

The provider id is `oauth:google`, and the default scopes are `openid email profile`.

The profile comes from Google's userinfo endpoint: `sub`, `email`, `name` and `picture` as `avatarUrl`. `emailVerified` is set only when Google answers `email_verified: true`, which makes `onFederationConflict: 'link-if-verified'` usable here.

The routes, the options every provider shares and account linking are on the [OAuth](/duck-auth/providers/oauth) page.

1. Create an application in the [Discord Developer Portal](https://discord.com/developers/applications).
2. Under **OAuth2**, add `https://app.example.com/auth/providers/oauth:discord/callback` as a redirect.
3. Copy the client id and secret.

```ts
import { discord } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/oauth/discord'

discord({
  clientId: process.env.DISCORD_CLIENT_ID ?? '',
  clientSecret: process.env.DISCORD_CLIENT_SECRET ?? '',
  redirectUri: 'https://app.example.com/auth/providers/oauth:discord/callback',
  stateSigningSecret: process.env.OAUTH_STATE_SECRET ?? '',
  nonceStore,
  profileToIdentityProfile: (p) => (p.email ? { email: p.email, username: `discord:${p.sub}`, name: p.name } : null),
})
```

The provider id is `oauth:discord`, and the default scopes are `identify email`.

* `sub` is the account's id, which survives a username change.
* `name` is the display name, else the username. `avatarUrl` is built from the avatar hash on Discord's CDN.
* `emailVerified` is set only when Discord answers `verified: true`.

The routes, the options every provider shares and account linking are on the [OAuth](/duck-auth/providers/oauth) page.

1. In [Certificates, Identifiers & Profiles](https://developer.apple.com/account/resources/identifiers/list), create a **Services ID** with **Sign in with Apple** enabled. Its identifier is your client id.
2. Configure it with your domain and the return URL `https://app.example.com/auth/providers/oauth:apple/callback`.
3. Under **Keys**, create a key with **Sign in with Apple** enabled and download the `AuthKey_<keyId>.p8`. Note the key id and your team id.

```ts
import { apple } from '@gentleduck/auth/providers/oauth/apple'

apple({
  clientId: 'com.example.app.web',
  teamId: process.env.APPLE_TEAM_ID ?? '',
  keyId: process.env.APPLE_KEY_ID ?? '',
  privateKey: process.env.APPLE_PRIVATE_KEY ?? '', // the .p8 contents
  redirectUri: 'https://app.example.com/auth/providers/oauth:apple/callback',
  stateSigningSecret: process.env.OAUTH_STATE_SECRET ?? '',
  nonceStore,
  profileToIdentityProfile: (p) => (p.email ? { email: p.email, username: `apple:${p.sub}`, name: p.name } : null),
})
```

The provider id is `oauth:apple`, and the default scopes are `name email`.

* There is no `clientSecret`. Each token exchange signs a fresh ES256 client secret from the key, valid for 30 minutes. `generateClientSecret` is exported if you need one elsewhere.
* Apple posts the callback as a form, so it needs the POST callback route on the [OAuth](/duck-auth/providers/oauth#the-routes) page, and a `secure` state cookie: the cookie goes out `SameSite=None`, and a non-secure one throws `AUTH_MISCONFIGURED`. Test over https.
* The profile is read from the id\_token. `emailVerified` is set when it says `email_verified` is `true` or `"true"`. A user who hides their address signs in with an `@privaterelay.appleid.com` one.
* Apple sends the name only on the first authorization. Store it from `profileToIdentityProfile`, since no later sign-in carries it.

The options every provider shares and account linking are on the [OAuth](/duck-auth/providers/oauth) page.
